SHRIMATI KANIMOZHI: Sir, in 1967, the DMK Government amended the Hindu 
Marriage Act and recognised marriages which are devoid of any religious ceremony as 
valid. The Chief Minister has also written to the Union Government for amending the Act on 
a national level. Will the Government consider this matter?
 
SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ: Sir, this issue comes under the Concurrent List. Mostly, the 
State Legislatures do take their own decision s within the States. There are several States 
which have already enacted laws and registration is provided there. But, since this matter 
was taken up by the Supreme Court, it was desired that there should be some sort of certainty 
about registration of women marriages to prot ect the interest of women. So, a concerted 
effort is being made to harmonise this law so that there is no difficulty in any faith or any 
religion, when the women suffer. They need protection of law and there should be presumption 
about the marriage and they should produce the certificate. This is a very laudable object. 
There is no need of any controversy.

Statement 
(a) to (d) No, Sir. The education system in India tries to promote merit and excellence,

social and economic priorities. Educational Reform is a continuing process and the Eleventh

spending. It is true that research efforts in our higher education system has a considerable 
scope for improvement. Increasing the number of Ph.Ds from Indian universities strengthening 
linkages between the universities and the Scientific Research Institutions, inclusion of greater 
research component in Post Graduate Programmes, promoting collaborative research among 
universities, strengthening of the research infrastructure, creation of research positions and 
enhancing fellowships, are integral to the reforms envisaged in the Eleventh Five Year Plan.

apprise the House that there is no one particular global system of education due to

research in the country.

SHRIGIREESH KUMAR SANGHI: 
Will the Minister of WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a UN report released says that malnutrition and child mortality continues to 
endanger the lives of children in the country and accounts for 50 per cent death of under five 
children and is also responsible for the low weight among children; 
(b) whether, according to report the country has to reach the Millennium Development 
Goal of 38 by 2015, the average annual rate of reduction in the next nine years has to be about 
7.6 per cent; 
(c) if so, the other main points mentioned in the UN report; and 
(d) the steps being considered for implementation of the report? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND CHILD 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MATI RENUKACHOWDHURY): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the 
Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) As per United Nations International Ch ildren's Emergency Fund (UNICEF) report 
titled "Progress for Children", N0.6, December, 2007, under five mortality rate in 2006 was 76 
per thousand live births in the country. 
The child mortality is not responsible for the low weight among children. Early marriages 
of girls, teenage pregnancies, poor health of pregnant ladies and malnutrition result in low 
birth weight of the new boms. Improper and poor breastfeeding and complementary feeding 
practices, ignorance about nutritional needs of infants and young children and repeated 
infections further aggravate the situation. 
(b) Yes, as per the report, the country has to reach the Millennium Development Goals 
target of under five mortality rate upto 38 per thousand live births by 2015 and accordingly 
the average annual rae of reduction has to be 7.6 percent during the period of 2007—2015. 
(c) The UNICEF report highlights the country specific Millennium Development Goals 
(MDG), their targets and the progress made by different countries. It also stresses the need 
to accelerate the progress in the following areas:

* MDG 4-Reduce Child Mortality. 
* MDG 5-Improve Maternal Health. 
* MDG 6-Combate HIV and AIDs, Malaria and other Diseases.

in national development if the MDGs are to be achieved. The Government is seized of the

directly or indirectly improve the nutritional status of women & children. Some of these are

Child Development);

services under ICDS includes:

from Re. 1 to Rs.2/- per beneficiary per day.

*154. SHRIT.T.V. DHINAKARAN: Will the Ministerof NEWAND RENEWABLE ENERGY

THE MINISTEROF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF NEW AND RENEWABLE ENERGY 
(SHRI VILAS MUTTEMWAR): (a) India receives solar energy equivalent to over 5,000 
trillion kWh per year. The daily average solar energy incident over India varies from 4-7 kWh 
per square meter depending upon the location. Solar energy can be harnessed through two 
routes, namely solar photovoltaic (PV) and solar thermal, by direct conversion to electricity 
and heat energy respectively. The utilization of solar energy in the country is currently 
limited, yet it is regularly inceasing. 
(b) The high initial cost of solar energy devices and systems, and lack of sufficient 
awareness are the main reasons for low utilization. However, some of the solar energy systems 
are becoming cost competitive to the conventional alternatives, when compared over the life 
of the systems. Solar water heaters, solar cookers and photovoltaic systems for small power 
applications in remote areas are the examples. 
(e) The Ministry has taken several steps to increase the utilization of solar energy in the 
country, which include (i) expanded programmes of the Mi nistry of encourage utilization 
of solar energy systems through subsidy or so ft loans, (ii) incen tive to manufacturers, 
commercial users and power project developers, (iii) research and development to reduce 
the cost, improve the efficiency  and performance of solar energy  systems, (iv) support of 
Akshaya Urja shops to provide additional chan nels for sale and after-sales servicing of 
solar energy systems, and (v) create awarene ss about the solar energy systems and their 
benefits.

Statement 
Copy of Relevant Extracts regarding revamping of AICTE 
"4. Regulation 
There is a clear need to establish an Independent Regulatory Authority for Higher Education 
(IRAHE). Such a regulatory authority is both necessary and desirable. 

48    Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Unstarred Questions 
It is necessary for two important reasons. First, in India, it requires an Act of Legislature 
of Parliament to set up a University. The deemed university route is much too difficult for 
new institutions. Entry through legislation alone, as at present, is a formidable barrier. The 
consequence is a steady increase in the average size of exis ting universities with a steady 
deterioration in their quality. The absence of competition only compounds problems. Second, 
as we seek to expend the higher education system, entry norms will be needed for private 
institutions and public-private parternships. The institutional framework for this purpose 
must be put in place here and now. 
It is desirable for four important reasons. First, it would minimize conflicts of interest as it 
would create an arm's-length distance from stakeholders. Second, it would replace the present 
system which is over-regulated but under-governed, through more appropriate forms of 
intervention. Third, it would rationalize the existing system where mandates are both 
confusing and overlapping. Fourth, it would disp ense with the multiplicity or regulatory 
agencies to provide a single-window  clearnace. 
The present regulatory system in higher education is flawed in many respects. The barriers 
to entry are too high. The system of authorizing entry is cumbersome and there are extensive 
rules after entry, as the UGC seeks to regulate almost every aspect of an institution from fees to 
curriculum....The other regulators, say in the sphere of professional education, are often 
inconsistent in their adherence to principles. There are several instances where an engineering 
college or a business school is approved, promptly in a small house of a metropolitan subrub 
without the requisite teachers, infrastructure or facilities, but established universities experience 
difficulties in obtaining similar approvals. Such examples can be multiplied. These would only 
confirm that the complexity, the multiplicity and the regidity of the existing regulatory structure 
is not conducive to the expansion of higher education opportunities in India. 
In sum, the existing regulatory framework constrains the supply of good institutions, 
excessively regulates existing institutions in  the wrong places, and is not conducive to 
innovation or creativity in higher education. The challenge is therefore to design a regulatory 
system that increases the supply of good in stitutions and fosters accountability in those 
institutions. An independent regulator has to be the cornerstone of such a system. 
The proposed IRAHE will rationalize the principles on which entry is regulated. There are 
two aspects to this rationalization: what is to be regulated and what are the principles used 
for regulation. 
In higher education, regulators perform five functions: (1) Entry: licence to grant degrees. 
(2) Accreditation: quality benchmarking. (3) Disbursement of public funds. (4) Access: fees 
or affirmative action. (5) Licence: to practice profession. 
India is perhaps the only country in the world where regulation in four of the five function 
is carried out by one entity, that is, the UGC. The purpose of creating an IRAHE is to separate 
these functions. The proposed IRAHE shall be reponsible for setting the criteria and deciding 
on entry. It would, in addition, license agencies to take care of accreditation. The role of the 
UGC will be limited to disbursing public funds, Issues of access will be governed by state 
legislation on reservation and other forms of affirmative action. And, professional association 
may, in some institutions, set requirements to determine eligibility for conducting a profession. 
All other regulatory agencies such as the AICTE will need to be abolished while the MCI 
and the BCI will be limited to their role as professional associations. These professional 

Written Answers to [10 MARCH, 2008] Unstarred Questions   49 
associations could conduct nationwide examinations to provide licence for those wishing to 
enter the profession. 
The second aspect of regulation is the principle use to regulate. The IRAHE will determine 
eligibility for setting up a new institution based on transparent criteria rather than discretionary 
controls. Its main role would be to exercise due diligence at the point it approves a licence to 
grant degrees. In doing so, it would assess the academic credibility and the financial viability 
of the proposed institution on the basis of information submitted in accordance with the 
stipulated criteria. It will apply exactly the same norms to public and private institutions, just 
as it will apply the same norms to domestic and international institutions. 
The IRAHE would have to be established by an Act of Parliament. It would be the only 
agency that would be author ized to accord degree granti ng power to higher education 
institutions. It would also be responsible for monitoring standards and settling disputes. It 
should also be thought of as the authority for licensing accreditation agencies. The IRAHE 
must be at am arm's length from the governemnt and independent of all stakeholders including 
the concerned Ministries of the Government. The Acts of the UGC, AICTE, MCI and BCI 
would have to be amended. The role of the UGC would be re-defined to focus on the 
disbursement of grants to, and maintenance of, public institutions in higher education. The 
entry regulatory functions of the AICTE, the MCI and the BCI would be performed by the 
IRAHE, so that their role would be limited to that of profession al associations. The 
professional associations could conduct nationwide examinations to provide license for 
those wishing to enter the profession."

Grants to Schools and Libraries 
t952. SHRI BANWARI LAL KANCHHAL: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government is aware that a book fair is organized after every two years at 
Pragati Maidan, New Delhi; 
(b) whether Government has taken notice of the fact that the publishers are disappointed 
and angry with the fact that no grants were  provided to the schools and libraries for 
purchasing books at the book fair held in 2008; 
(c) whether Government would .make any arrangement to allow free entry in the world 
book fair and provide grants to the schools and libraries in order to solve these hardships in 
future; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCEBEVELORMENT 
(SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI): (a) Yes Sir. New Delhi World Book Fair is organized 
every alternate year at Pragati Maidan, New Delhi by The National Book Trust, India, an 
autonomous organisation of the Ministry of Human Resource Development. 
(b) The Government has not received any representation from the publishers in this 
regard. 
(c) and (d) Entry fee in the Pragati Maidan is charged by the India Trade Promotion 
Organisation (ITPO). However, the National Book Trust, India had requested ITPO to 
exempt the entry fee during the 18th New Delhi World Book Fair held during 2nd February 
2008 to 10th February 2008. ITPO announced entry fee concession for school children 
accompanied by their teachers and for schools as well as college libraries. The Central 
Government does not provide grants directly to colleges and schools and has no role in 
deciding on where from educational institutions should purchase books for libraries.

Functioning of AICTE 
953. SHRI TARIQ ANWAR: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a question has been raised on the functioning of All India 
Council for Technical Education on various issues; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it also a fact that some colleges get affiliation very easily and some reputed 
colleges are not getting if; and 
(d) if so, what action Government would take in this regard? 
THE MINISTEROF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT 
(SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI):  (a) and (b) The Government has been receiving 
representations on the functioning of All Indian Council for Technical Education (AICTE) on 
various issues like: 
(i) Delay in grant of approval, 
(\'\J Restrictive policy in approval of new courses and expansion in intake, of existing 
courses, 
(iii) Lack of uniformity in applying norms and standards in grant of approval, 
(iv) Delay in payment of M. Tech. Scholarship, 
(v) Lack of action by AICTE on complaints against institutions relating to malpractices 
in admissions, and 
(vi) Irregularities in Regional Offices. 
(c) Affiliation is granted by universities and not by AICTE 
(d) Does not arise. 
Introduction of sex education in schools 
954. DR. K. MALAISAMY: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether much debate is going on about introduction of sex education in schools; 
(b) what are all the plus and minus points of this issue; and 
(c) what is the policy of Government and its initiatives on this? 
THE MINISTEROF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT 
(SHRI MD. ALIASHRAF FATMI): (a) to (c) Ministry of Human Resource Development in 
collaboration with National AIDS Control Organization (NACO) has launched "Adolescence 
Education Programme (AEP)" for implementation by all the State and Union Territory 
Governments. 
The framework of the Progra mme incorporates three majo r concerns of adolescence; 
(i) Process of Growing up during adolescence, (ii) Prevention of HIV/AIDS and (iii) Prevention 
of Substance (Drug) Abuse. The programme is meant for the students of secondary and 
higher secondary schools and is an effort to help the students acquire life skills so that they 

Written Answer to [10 MARCH. 2008] Unstarred Questions   79 
avoid risky situations and take informed decisions and develop healthy and responsible 
behavior. 
In view of some criticism in media regarding appropriateness of the material used in the 
programme, National AIDS Control Organization (NACO) of the Ministry of Health & Family 
Welfare (MOHFW) has set up a Committee to review the material pertaining to Adolescence 
Education Programme. Besides, all the States and Union Territories have also been advised 
to review the material to align the same in the context of local environment and socio-cultural 
ethos. 
Restriction on deemed universities to conduct examinations 
955. SHRI S.S. AHLUWALIA: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether University Grants Commission (UGC) has proposed new guidelines to debar 
deemed universities from conducting under-graduate and distance learning courses, restricting 
only to masters level courses for them; 
(b) if so. the details thereof; 
(c) the details of deemed universities alongwith the details of under-graduate courses 
conducted presently, by them on regular and through distance learning mode, in the country; 
(d) the rationale behind the proposal; 
(e) whether responsibility of regulating distance learning education vests with the. Distance 
Education Council under IGNOU or with UGC; and 
(f) whether the UGC's proposal has been vetted by the Council? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT 
(SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI): (a) and (b) No, Sir. There is no such proposal with the 
Central Government at present. According to the University Grants Commission (UGC), the 
draft UGC (Institutions Deemed-to-be-Universities) Regulations 2008, are presently only at 
the consultation stage. 
(c) Details of the undergraduate courses conducted by the deemed-to-be-universities are 
not maintained centrally. The State-wise details of institutions that have been declared as 
'deemed-to-be-universities' under Section 3 of the UGC Act, 1956 are enclosed as Statement. 
(See below). 
(d) In view of the reply to parts (a) and (b) above, does not arise. 
(e) Distance Education Council (DEC), a statutory authority under the IGNOU Act 1985, is 
responsible for promotion, coordination and maintenance of standards of open and distance 
education system in the country. Institutions declared as deemed-to-be-universities, could 
offer distance education programmes only with the specific approval of the DEC and the 
UGC. Accordingly, all proposals submitted by the deemed-to-be-universities to start distance 
education have to be approved by both the DEC and the UGC. 
(f) Does not arise in view of reply to parts (a) and (b) above.

Powers of regulatory bodies 
956. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: 
SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: 
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the National Knowledge Commission has urged Government to curtail the 
powers of the regulatory bodies for higher education; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether the Commission has submitted a detailed report to Government in this regard; 
(d) if so, the details of the recommendations made by the Commission; and 
(e) the further reaction of Government on those rcommendations? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT 
(SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI): (a) to (e) In its Report to the Nation (2206), the National 
Knowledge Commission (NKC) has recommended establishment of an Independent 
Regulatory Authority for Higher Education and re-defining the role of regulatory bodies 
such as University Grants Commission (UGC), All India Council for Technical Education 
(AICTE), Medical Council of India (MCI) and Bar Council of India (BCI). No decision has 

Written Answer to [10 MARCH, 2008] Unstarred Questions   85 
been taken on the recommendations of NKC. However, a Review Committee has been 
constituted by Government to review the functions of the UGC and AICTE.

NKC recommendations for higher and primary education 
958. SHRIMATI MOHSINA KIDWAI: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) how many recommendations relating to higher and primary education have been given 
by the National Knowledge Commission, so far; 
(b) what are the details of those recommendations, item-wise; 
(c) how many recommendations have been implemented by Government; and 
(d) how many recommendations have not been accepted, alongwith the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI): (a) and (b) The recommendations 
given by the National Knowledge Commission in respect of Higher and Primary 
education include; 
Higher Education: 
1. To create more-universities. 
2. To change the system of regulation for higher education. 
3. To increase public spending and diversify sources of financing. 
4. To establish 50 National Universities. 
5. To reform existing universities. 
6. To restructure undergraduate colleges. 
7. To promote enhanced quality.

8. To ensure access for all deserving students. 
Primary Education: 
1. Planning for School Infrastructure. 
2. Enabling and regulating mechanisms for private schools. 
3. Database on school education. 
4. National Evaluation body for monitoring. 
5. Revamping school inspection. 
6. Teachers and teacher training. 
7. English language teaching. 
These are also available in the Pl anning Commission's web-site namely; http:// 
planningcommission.nic.in and http://www.knowledgecommission.gov.in 
(c) and (d) Some of the recommendations have already been included as proposals in the 
Xlth Plan and some recommendations are under consideration. 
Violent incidents in schools 
t959. PROF. RAM DEO BHANDARY: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that, due to mutual enmity and groupism among school students in 
different parts of the country, violent incidents have increased, in which some students have 
died and others got serious injuries; 
(b) if so, the details of incidents that occurred in different schools of the country during 
the last two years; and 
(c) the reasons therefor and the efforts Government are making to stop this? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALIASHRAF FATMI): (a) to (c) Some sporadic instances of 
violence among school students have been reported in the media recently. Education is a 
concurrent subject and school education primarily comes under the purview of the 
respective State Governments. Details of violent incidents in schools are not maintained 
centrally. The reasons for such violence could be due to disturbances in the psycho-social 
domain of the children and changing societal behaviour. In schools under Central 
Government, such as Kendriya Vidyalayas, the school based Discipline Committees have 
been assigned pro-active role and such problems are addressed through guidance and 
counselling activities.

Cheap and diluted system in SSA 
 
961. SHRI KAMAL AKHTAR: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether SSA is nothing but a cut-rate system of education where focus is on doing 
everything cheap and standards have been diluted for practically everything, from ratio of 
teachers to a school to curiculum that is offered; 
(b) whether elementary education is now reduced to eight years instead of 12, which the 
experts say is absolutely essential for children to find a right career; 
 
(c) whether, in SSA, there are no teachers put para teachers-ill-qualified, people,    
unemployed village youth, who get a pittance and are termed as Shiksha Karmis, etc; and 
(d) if so, the changes proposed in the SSA, to make it more focused and result-oriented? 
♦ THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCED 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALIASHRAF FATMI): (a) No, Sir. The Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan 
(SSA) programme  which aims to achieve the objective of universalisation of elementary 
education, is being implemented in all districts of al l States/UTs of the country with 
sharing of funds between the Central and the State/UT Governments. Teacher recruitment 
and curriculum, which are State subjects, are done/implemented as per respective 
State/UT-specific policies. 
(b) As per the National Policy on Education (NPE), 1986(as modified in 1992), a common 
educational structure 10+2+3 is envisaged. Regarding further break-up of the first 10 years, 
NPE provides that "efforts will be made to move towards an elementary system comprising

5 years of primary education and three years of upper primary, followed by 2 years of High 
School. Efforts will also be made to have th e +2 stage accepted as a part of the school 
education throughout the country". Thus, the elementary education system comprises of 
eight years of schooling as per the postulates of NPE, 1986 as modified in 1992. 
(c) and (d) As per District Information System for Education (DISE) 2006-07 data, out of 
52.18 lakh teachers at elementary level only 9.86% are para teachers.

Intensification of Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan 
t967. DR. PRABHA THAKUR: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
tOriginal notice of the question was received in Hindi. 

Written Answer to [10 MARCH, 2008] Unstarred Questions   97 
(a) what effective steps are being taken by Government to intensify Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan 
in rural areas of various States of the country; 
(b) whether Government is getting any financial assistance therefor from international 
financial institutions; 
(c) if so, the details thereof and from which institutions institution financial assistance 
has been received during the last three years and in which States that assistance has been 
used; 
(d) the status of various States engaged in effective implementation of the scheme; 
(e) whether Central Government monitors the functioning of States and if so, the details 
thereof; and 
(f) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT 
(SHRI MD. ALI ASHRAF FATMI): (a) to (f) The Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA) programme 
is being implemented in all districts of the country to achieve the goal of universalisation of 
elementary education in a mission mode. Various incentives including cooked mid day meal 
are being provided to ensure unversal enrolment of children in rural areas, in the 6—14 years 
age group. Consequently 98% of rural India has a primary school within one kilometer and 
remaining rural habitations have alternate schooling arrangements including Education 
Gurantee Scheme (EGS). 
World Bank (WB), Department for International Development (DFID) of United 
Kingdom and European Commission (EC) have been providing partial financial assistance 
for the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA) on reimbursement basis. Total reimbursements 
claimed by Government of India from these agen cies in the last thr ee years i.e. 2004-05, 
2005-06 & 2006-07 have been Rs. 1047.67 crore, Rs. 2341.98 crore&Rs. 1091.91 crore, 
respectively. Government of India has so far received an amount of Rs. 189.88 crores in 
2007-08 as reimbursement from external funding agencies on account of the Sarva Shiksha 
Abhiyan. 
Central funds under Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan are released to all State/UTs on the basis of 
Annual Work Plan and Budget (AWP&B) submitted by State/UTs to the Government of 
India every year. A part of this expenditure of Government of India is reimbursed by external 
funding agencies. 
A rigorous system of monitoring of the SSA for tracking the performance of States, is in 
place which includes, inter-alia, monthly and quarterly progress reports and review meetings, 
furnishing of annual elementary school statistics, field monitoring by 40 independent monitoring 
institutions and six monthly-independent Review Missions. In addition, annual statutory audit 
of the State/UT SSA programmes are in place and concurrent financial reviews are also carried 
out. Wherever deficiencies in the implementation of the programme are noticed, such deficiencies 
are brought to the notice of the State Governments for corrective action.

Rigid system of education 
977. SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR RE DDY: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the present study system is rigid and mostly students mug up 
their lessons without knowing well the background of the subject or the other connecting 
links to it; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) why Government is not taking the corrective steps and playing with the future of 
valuable students? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT 
(SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI): (a) to (c) In order to address the problem of information 
overload on children without any regard to their age, ability or time available in school as 
pointed out in a Report entitled "Learning without Burden", the National Curriculum 
Framework-2005 has suggested: 
(i) Connecting knowledge to life outside the school, 
(ii) Ensuring that learning is shifted away from rote methods, 
(iii) Enriching the curriculum to provide for overall development of children rather 
than remain textbook centre, 
(iv) Making examinations more flexible and integrated into classroom life, and 
(v) Nurturing an overriding identity informed by caring concerns within the democratic 
policy of the country. 
In Higher Education, the University Grants Commission is undertaking academic reforms 
during the eleventh Plan in regard to assessment/evaluation procedure, examination reforms 
like credit system, semester system, continuous and internal evaluation.

Criminal cases against politicians 
996. DR. V. MAITREYAN: Will the Minister of LAW AND JUSTICE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) the total number of crim inal cases pending against the present politicians 
holding posts, as well as former politicians across the country, State-wise; 
(b) the action being taken to dispose of the pending cases with clear verdicts; 
(c) whether it is a fact that many cases are pending for a long time and they are not 
coming up for hearing due to manipulations in the court procedures; and 
(d) if so, the steps being taken to monitor the pending cases for speedy justice? 
THE MINISTER OP LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ): (a) to (d) 
The Department of Justice does not maintain data on the number of criminal cases 
pending against politicians. However, during the last year, the Department-related 
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personne l, Public Grievances, Law and Justice 
while studying the matter of 'Electoral Reforms' is seized of the matter relating to 
charge-sheet files against sitting MPs/MLAs in different competent courts of law. In 
order to provide information to the said Committee, all State Governments and UT 
Administrations were requested to provide the same. Some States/UTs have furnised the 
requisite information. As per available information, there are around 1300 cases 
pending against sitting MPs/MLAs in various courts, as on 31.3.2007. Further, CBI has 
reported that it is investigating around 65 such cases. 
As regards manipulations in the court procedures, it may be mentioned that the 
judiciary is independent and as such the Government cannot interfere with the functions 
of the ' judiciary. 
The dispoal of criminal trials in the courts takes considerable time and that in many 
cases trials do not commence for as long a period as 3 to 5 years after the accused was 
remitted to judicial custody. Large number of persons accused of criminal offences have 
not been able to secure bail for one reason or  the other and have to languish in jail as 
under-trial prisoners for years. To reduce the delay in the disposal of criminal trials and 
appeals and also to alleviate the suffering of under-trial prisoners, the concept of plea-
bargaining was introduced in the Code of Criminal Procedure 1973.

Mining concessions 
1004. SHRI EKANATH K. THAKUR: Will the Minister of MINES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that out of 260 iron mines, for which the Ministry has approved 
mineral concessions during the period between 2001 to 2007,172 went to merchant miners 
mainly for export purpose which is not in the national interest; 

Written Answers to [10 MARCH, 2008] Unstarred Questions    121 
(b) whether it is also a fact that an exportcess of Rs. 300 levied on per tonne of iron ore is 
virtually nothing compared to the rise in spot market iron ore prices; and 
(c) if so, the steps Government proposes to take to protect and conserve iron ore reserves 
in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF MINES (DR. T. SUBBARAMIREDDY): 
(a) Under the National Mineral Policy in 1993, mining for non-fuel and non-atomic minerals 
has been thrown open for private sector investment and an Indian National or a Company as 
defined in sub-section 3(1) of the Companies Act, 1956 can undertake mining based on the 
economic viability of the project. Mining is a stand-alone activity. The Central Government, 
based on the State Governmnet recommendations, accords prior approval for grant of mineral 
concessions in terms of the provisions of the Mines and Minerals (Development and 
Regulation) Act, 1957 and Rules framed there under. The export of minerals including iron ore 
is as per the EXIM policy of the Government. 
(b) The levy of export cess is a fiscal measure by Government and not linked to the 
movement of spot prices of iron ore. 
(c) The Government is of the view that management of mineral resources is closely 
integrated with the overall strategy of development of minerals whereby exploitation of 
minerals is to be guided by long-term natio nal goals and perspectives. The country has 
sufficient resources of iron ore at 25.25 billion tonnes and these are increasing with further 
exploration.

Shortage of power 
1015. SHRI DARA SINGH: 
SHRI RAMDAS AGARWAL: 
Will the Minister of NEW AND RENEWABLE ENERGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the country faces acute shortage of  energy and is spending more than Rs. 
1,00,000 crore on power generation and distribution; 
(b) whether solar energy holds the key for power-hungry India, but the same has not 
been adequately tapped; 
(c) what concrete steps Government has taken so far to tap the sun for energy, when 
advanced solar energy technologies are available; and 
(d) the details of Government's plans for expansion and utilization of solar energy 
resources for domestic and commercial purposes during the Eleventh Five Year Plan? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF NEW AND RENEWABLE ENERGY 
(SHRI VILAS MUTTEMWAR): (a) to (d) Yes, Sir. There is gap in the demand and supply of 
power in the country. The renewable energy sources such as wind, small hydro and biomass 
have contributed about 11274 MW to the capacity addition of power generation in the 
country. 
India received solar energy e quivalent to over 5,000 tril lion KWh per year. The daily 
average solar energy incident over India varies from 4-7 kwh per square meter depending 
upon the location. Solar energy can be harnessed through two routes, namely solar 
photovoltaic (PV) and solar thermal, by direct conversion to electricity and heat energy 
respectively, Thus solar energy has potential to meet growing demand of energy. The high 
initial cost of solar energy devices and systems, and lack of sufficient awareness are the main 
reasons for low utilization of this resource. However, some of the solar energy systems are 
becoming cost competitive to the conventional alternatives, when compared over the life of 
the systems. Solar water heaters, solar cook ers and photovoltaic systems for small power 
applications in remote areas are the examples. 
The Ministry has taken several steps to incr ease the utilization of solar energy in the 
country during the 11th plan, which include (i) expanded programme of the Ministry to 
encourage utilization of solar energy systems through subsidy or soft loans, (ii) incentive 
to manufacturers, commercial users and pow er project developers , (iii) research and 
development to reduce the cost, improve the efficiency and performance of solar energy 
systems, and (iv) support to Akshya Urja shops to provide additional channels for sale 
and after-sales servicing of solar energy systems and (v) create awareness about the solar 
energy systems and their benefits.

Working of APDRP 
1020. DR. K. MALAISAMY: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) when the Accelerated Power Development Reforms Programme (APDRP) was introduced 
and what is the impact of the programme on States; 
(b) whether it is a fact that many States including Tamil Nadu, despite the incentive given 
in this Scheme, did not complete the works as per schedule but extended them for years; 
(c) if so, what are the specific reasons for such abnormal delay in execution; 
(d) whether it is also a fact that there has been diversion of APDRP funds for unauthorized 
purposes and incorrect reporting of expenditure by States; and 
(e) if so, the effective system introduced to arrest the wrong practices in existence? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHILKUMAR SHINDE):(a) Government had 
launched Accelerated Power Development and Reforms Programme (APDRP) in the year 
2002-03 with the objective of encouraging reforms and of reduction in Aggregate Technical 
and Commercial (AT&C) loss, improving quality of supply of power and improving consumer 
satisfaction. The target was to reduce AT&C losses to 15% in five years to begin with in 
urban and high density consumption areas. AT&C loss has come down in towns where 
APDRP has been implemented. Further, some of the utilities which adopted various 
interventions as envisaged under the programme have shown significant reduction in AT&C 
loss. At town level, AT&C losses have been brought below 20 per cent in 215 APDRP towns 
in the country of which 163 towns have brought AT&C losses below 15 percent. 
(b) Government of lndia had sanctioned projects amounting to Rs. 17033.58 crore under the 
investment component for strengthening and upgradation of sub-transmission and distribution 
systems of the States. The States have so far utilized Rs. 11279.50 crores. State of Tamil Nadu 
has utilized Rs. 724.14 crores out of the total sanctioned cost of Rs. 948.12 crores. 
(c) There are delays in comple tion of the projects. The va rious reasons for delay in 
execution of projects are:

(i) Delay in processing the Notice Inviting Tender (NIT) for awarding the contacts by 
utilities. 
(ii) Delay in awarding the contracts by utilities. 
(iii) Delay in supply of equipments due to increased demand. 
(iv) Poor response from the contractors, especially in North-Eastern states and Jammu & 
Kashmir. 
(v) Delay in transfer of fund to the utilities by the States. 
(vi) Heavy quantum of work which utilities were not geared up to handle. 
(vii) Non-adoption of turnkey contract system by many utilities. 
(d) and (e) Comptroller and Auditor General of India (C&AG's) in its Report No. 16 of 2007 for the 
year ended March ' 2006 Union Government (Civil-Performance Audit) relating to "Performance 
Audit of Accelerated Power Development and Reforms Programme (APDRP)" has pointed out that 
there have been instances of diversion of funds and incorrect financial reporting by some of the 
States. 
In view of the recommendations/suggestions of the various stakeholders including C&AG 
on the implementation of APDRP, the programme is proposed to be restructured with the revised 
terms and conditions during the Eleventh Five Year Plan to make it more effective.

Power shortage in Eastern India 
1026. MS. SUSHILA TIRIYA: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that eastern India once had surplus power and is now on the verge 
of major crisis; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; and 

146    Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Unstarred Questions 
(c) the steps taken in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE): (a) to (c) The Surplus 
power used to be available on a sustained basis in the Eastern Region (ER). During the 
current year, (April, 2007 to January, 2008) th e energy and peak shor tage in the Eastern 
Region has been of the order of 4.6% and 6% respectively. As compared to the Eastern 
Region the energy and peak shortage in the country as a whole is of the order of 9% and 
15.2% respectively. The main reasons for shortage of power  in the Eastern Region are 
inadequate capacity addition within the Regi on vis-a-vis the growth in demand, poor 
performance of generating units in some of the States and reduced availability of power 
during the winter months due to reduction to water inflows into Tala Hydro Power Stations. 
After meeting held in the Central Electricity Authority (CEA) with the constituent 
States/Utilities of the Eastern Region at New Delhi on 30th January, 2008, the CEA has 
forwarded detailed recommendations to the Ministry of Power, which are given below: 
(i) 153 MW of Tala unallocated power may be continued to Northern Region. 
(ii) Restoration of 343 MW from Farakka and Kahalgaon Stage-I to Eastern Region 
Constituents by equivalent diversion (of 343 MW) fr om Kahalgaon State-II be 
done in phases as and when Kahalgaon-Il units 5,6 and 7 become operational. 
(iii) 150 MW from Kejia Unit 5 may be supplied by DVC to command area/Jharkhand/ 
West Bengal immediately on commissioning of the Unit. 
(iv) 150 MW from Mejia Unit 6 after commissioning of the Unit may be swapped with 
Kahalgaon State-I and Farakka Power. 
Power Sharing Agreement 
1027. SHRIO.TLEPCHA: 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGROD1A: 
Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether any agreement was signed between the Union Government and the State 
Governments of Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan regarding sharing of power generated in 
hydel power projects of Punjab; 
(b) if so, whether the share of Rajasthan has been finalized in respect of projects covered 
under the agreement; 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor; 
(d) whether the Union Government proposes to refer the claims of Rajasthan for power 
sharing in hydel project of Punjab to the Supreme Court; and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor and the steps being taken to expedite the finalization of 
Rajasthan's share in the projects mentioned in the agreement? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE): (a) to (e) An agreement 
was reached between the States of Punjab, Haryana & Rajasthan and Government of India 
on 10.05.1984 wherein it was agreed that in view of the claims raised by Haryana & Rajasthan 
for sharing of power in Anandpur Sahib Hydel Project, Mukerian Hydel Project, Thein Dam 
project, UBDC State-II and Shahpur Kandi hydel Scheme, the Government of India shall refer 

Written Answers to [10 MARCH, 2008] Unstarred Questions    147 
the matter to the Hon'ble Supreme Court for its opinion. The opinion of the Hon'ble Supreme 
Court was to be sought on whether the States of Rajasthan & Haryana are entitled to a share in 
the power generated from these hydel schemes and in case they are, what would be the 
share of each State. 
However, subsequently in the discussions held between the Chief Ministers of Punjab, Haryana 
and Rajasthan on 29-30 July, 1992 and 6th August, 1992, a consensus was reached not to refer the 
matter to the Hon'ble Supreme Court. It was also decided that the States would come to a 
reasonable agreement through mutual consultations. In order to resolve the issue amicably, a 
number of formal and informal discussions have taken place. However, no consensus has emerged 
so far due to the divergent views of the stakeholder States. Meanwhile, the State of Punjab has 
enacted the 'Punjab Termination of Agreements Act 2004', terminating and discharging the 
Government of Punjab from its obligations under the agreement between Punjab, Haryana and 
Rajasthan dated 31.12.1981 on reallocation of waters and under all other agreements relating to 
waters of Ravi-Beas. Government of India has made a Presidential Reference to the Supreme 
Court inter alia whether the Punjab Termination of Agreements Act, 2004 and the provisions 
thereof are in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution of India. 
National electricity fund 
1028. SHRI D. RAJA: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government is contemplating to create a National Electricity Fund to support 
the State Electricity Boards; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and by when the fund is likely to be made available to the 
t SEBs; 
(c) whether Government intends to initiate some other steps to strengthen the cash-
strapped SEBs; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE): (a) and (b) The Planning 
Commission has intimated that the Eleventh Plan document, approved by the National 
Development Council, has inter-alia recommended the setting up of a National Electricity 
Fund for supportive measures to bring about major improvement in the distribution system. It 
has been decided that Planning Commission will explore the option of establishing a National 
Electricity Fund to provide soft loans to States to improve their disribution infrastructure. 
(c) and (d) It is proposed to introduce a restructured Accelerated Power Development and 
Reforms Programme (APDRP) in the 11th Plan with a focus on establishing base line data in 
• respect of Aggregate Technical and Commercial (AT&C) losses, sanctioning projects for 
improvement of distribution network and incentivising utilities which achieve AT&C loss reduction.

Implementation of RGGVY in Bihar 
t1030. SHRI MANGANI LAL MANDAL: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) what has been the outcome of implementation of Rajiv Gandhi Grameen Vidyutikafan 
Yojana in Bihar as on date; 
(b) the targets achieved, so far, under the scheme for electrification of the targeted villages 
and what has been the physical and financial position as to the total cost incurred on, the said 
scheme; 
(c) whether it is a fact that Madhubani district is the most neglected district covered under 
this scheme and the areas, falling under Khutonna, Lookaha, Ghoghardiha and Phulparas 
Blocks and several villages like Sudyahi andGhoonsahi, etc-have not been included in this 
scheme at any stage so far; and 
(d) if so, what are the details in that regard? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE): (a) Bihar Government * 
has submitted44 DPRs covering electrification of 14195 un-electrified villages, re-electrification 
of 10508 de-electrified villages and intensive electrification of 6069 electrified villages with an 
outlay of Rs. 3345.68 crore. 
(b) The implementing agencies have reported  that electrification works in 12104 un- 
electrified villages (commulatively) have been carried out as on 15th February, 2O08. They 
have also reported release of 66799 rural household connections, including 52817 BPL 
household connections in Bihar under RGGVY. Bihar State so far(as on 25th February, 2008) 
have availed Rs. 1288.23 crore under RGGVY. 
(c) and (d) NHPC, the implementing agencyof RGGVY project in Madhubani district, with 
concurrence of Bihar Government, has submitted two DPRs, one covering electrification of 
16 un-electrified villages and re-electrification of 310 de-electrified viIlages under "Accelerated 
Electrification of One Lakh Villages and One Crore Households" which now stands merged   - 
with RGGVY. This project was sanctioned in March 2005. 
Subsequently, NHPC has submitted supplementary DPR of Madhubani district covering 
electrification of 221 un-electrified villages, re-electrification of 27 de-electrified villages and 
intensive electrification of 459 already electrified villages which is yet to be approved. 
Out of  the four blocks, three blocks namely Lookana,Ghoghardiha and Phulparas find 
coverage in both the DPRs whereas Khutonna is not appearing in either of the DPRs. 
tOriginal notice of the question was received in Hindi. 

Written Answers to [10 MARCH, 2008] Unstarred Questions    163 
However, village Khutonna with census code No. 0040200 has been covered in the 
supplementary DPR of Madhubani district. 
Sudyahi and Ghoonsahi villages have also not been covered in both these DPRs. 
Autonomy to NTPC 
1031. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government has decided to give more powers to NTPC, to 
enable it compete with private sector corporate projects; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the extent to which additional financia l powers would increase responsibility and 
accountability of NTPC? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHILKUMAR SHINDE): (a) and (b) NTPC Ltd. is 
a Navaratna Public Sector Undertaking which has been granted enhanced autonomy as per 
Navaratna guidelines. According to the existing delegation of powers applicable to Navaratna 
Companies, the ceiling on equity investment to establish financial joint ventures and wholly 
owned subsidiaries in India or abroad shall be 15% of the net worth of the Public Sector 
Enterprise (PSE) in one project limited to Rs. 1000 crore and the overall ceiling on such 
investment in all projects put together shall be 30% of the net worth of the PSE. Government 
of India in November, 2006 had granted waiver of ceiling of Rs. 1000 crore for equity investment 
by NTPC Ltd. to establish financial joint ventures and wholly owned subsidiaries for the 
purpose of participating in the bidding of Ultra Mega Projects subject to the implementation 
of maximum of two projects. 
(c) In the changing power sector scenario which is going through a massive expansion 
phase, NTPC Limited has to resort to the joint venture mode! for many of its projects to 
contribute to a substantial share of power generation in the country. The enhanced/additional 
financial delegated powers would further consolidate NTPC's position as the leading thermal 
power generation company in India and abroad. The responsibility and accountability of 
NTPC will also increase to the extent of the actua exereise additional financial powers. 
Approval for Gundia Hydro Electric Project 
1032. SHRI RAJEEV CHANDRASEKHAR: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether a proposal for setting up of Gundia Hydro Electric Project in Hassan district of 
Karnataka is pending with the Central Electricity Authority for approval; and 
(b) if so, the present status of the case and by when the approval to the project is likely to 
be accorded? 

164    Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Unstarred Questions 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHILKUMAR SHINDE): (a) and (b) No Sir. The 
Central Electricity Authority (CEA) have informed that no proposal for concurrence of Gundia 
Hydro Electric Project in Hassan  District of Karnataka is pending with them for approval. 
However, CEA have also informed that the Detailed Project Report (DPR) of Gundia Hydro 
Electric Project (2 x 200 MW), located in Hassan and Dakshina Kannada District of Karnataka 
was submitted by Karnataka Power Corporation Ltd. (KPCL) to CEA in July, 2006 for 
concurrence. In the absence of essential inputs/clearances, the DPR could not be processed' 
for concurrence and was returned to KPCL by CEA on 11.08.2006. An Addendum to the DPR 
was submitted by KPCL in October, 2007 which had major changes from the original DPR. 
KPCL envisaged development of the project in two Phases; KPCL also changed the type of 
Turbine from Francis to Pelton wheel. Some of the Geological investigations were also not 
carried out by KPCL. Due to non-resolution of various issues, the DPR was again returned to 
KPCL on 17.01.2008 with the request that revised DPR may be submitted to CEA after 
carrying out the requisite Geological investigations and incorporating the necessary changes 
and resolution of various outstanding issues.

through adjustment of allocation generally within the States/UTs in the region keeping in

Status of power supply 
t 11038. SHRI AJAY SINGH CHAUTALA: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the supply of power in the country, particularly in Haryana, is 
erratic, the power grids are defective and regular supply of coal is not made to the thermal 
power stations; 
(b) whether the people have to face large scale shortage of power supply as a result 
thereof; and 
(c) the effective steps Government proposes to take to regularize the supply of power, 
check continuous defects in the power grids and ensure regular supply of coal to thermal 
power stations? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE): (a) and (b) There is a 
continuing overall shortage of power in the country including Haryana. The quantum of 
shortage varies from State to State, on day to day and hour to hour basis depending on 
demand and, supply of power. The energy and peak shortage in the country during the 
current year (April, 2007-January, 2008) was 9.0% and 15.2% respectively. The energy and 
peak shortage in Haryana during the current year was 11% and 2.7% respectively. 
For ensuring proper supply of power, adequate transmission system under central sector 
has been provided/planned in Haryana. About 3065 MVA transformation capacity at 400 kV 
under central sector and 1400 MVA Bhakra Beas Management Board(BBMB) is operational 
in Haryana along with matching 400 kV transmission lines. A transformation capacity of 
about 3890 MVA at 400 kV has been approved and is likely to be available to the state within 
the next 3 to 4 years. 
The supply of coal to thermal power stations in the country including those of Haryana is 
being made on a regular basis and no loss of ge neration due to shortage of coal has been 
reported by Haryana during 2007-08 (upto February, 2008). 
(c) Electricity is a concurrent subject under the Constitution. The Supply and distribution 
of electricity in a State/UT is within the purview of the respective State Government/State 
Power Utilities. 
The steps taken/being taken to improve the supply of power in the country include 
augmentation of generating capacity by over 78,500 MW during the 11th Plan, development 
of Ultra Mega Power Projects of 4,000 MW capacity each, improving performance of existing 
power stations, renovation, modernization and life extension of old and inefficient generating 
units, harnessing surplus captive power into the grid, strengthening inter-state and inter-
regional transmission capacity for optimum utilization of available power, promoting demand 
side management, energy efficiency and energy conservation measures and import of power 
from Bhutan. 
In order to ensure regular supply of coal to the thermal power stations (TPSs) the 
production, transportation and stocking of coal at all the major TPSs, is being rigorously 
monitored to review and resolve the constraints.

Prime Minister's views on power situation 
1039. SHRI MATI SHOBHANABHARTIA: 
SHRIVIJAY J.DARDA: PROF. 
ALKABALRAM KSHATRIYA: 
Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Prime Minister has expressed serious concern over the power situation 
and proposed setting the agenda for power reforms in the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether there is marginal increase in the generation capacity and slow progress in 
augmentation of transmission and distribution networks; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) what concrete steps Government has sinc e taken to increase the power generation 
capacity and to remove various obstacles? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE): (a) to (d) Electricity is a 
concurrent subject under the Constitution. Ther efore, the Government of India has been 
discussing power sector issues with the St ates from time to time. Addressing the Chief 
Ministers in the Conference of the Chief Ministers convened by the Ministry of Power on 
28th May, 2007, the Prime Minister expressed concern, inter-alia, on the poor progress in the 
addition to generation capacity, in cutting do wn transmission & distribution losses, in 
reducing wasteful consumption and in attracting adequate private investment in power 
sector. A copy of the resolution adopted by the Conference expressing resolve of the Centre 
and the States to address various issues in the power sector is given in the enclosed 
Statement. (See below). 
The highest capacity addition in one year so far was 6853 M W in 2006-07. As against that 
during the year 2007-08, so far (upto 22.2.2008), the capacity of 7683 MW has already been 
added. 
As far as inter-state transmission is concerned, the development of transmission network 
is in tandem with the growth in generation capacity addition and all transmission projects 
associated with generation projects are being implemented by Powergrid matching with 
commissioning of generation projects. Intra-State transmission and distribution comes in 
the purview of the States. 
(e) Following steps have been taken by the Government to ensure timely completion of 
power generation projects: 
(i) Expediting letter of Award (LoA) in respect of 11th Plan projects in the first year of 
the 11th Plan itself.

(ii) Removal of constraints in meeting the main plant supplies for thermal projects, 
(iii) Addressing the issue related to availability of Balance of Plant (BoP) requirements, 
(iv) Overcoming shortage of manpower. 
(v) Regular monitoring of generation capacity addition targets. 
Statement 
Copy of the Resolution adopted by the Chief Ministers' Conference on Power 
(28th May, 2007) 
1. The Conference recognizes the vital importance of the power sector in the development 
of the economy which is on a trajectory of high growth and resolves that a time bound closely 
monitored action programme for accelerated cap acity addition, drastic loss reduction, 
achievement of the rural electrification targets set out under Bharat Nirman, and promotion of 
efficient energy and Demand Side Management, be put in place at the Centre and in the States. 
2. The Conference acknowledges that electricity is a concurrent subject. The States and 
the Centre shall jointly endea vour to provide access to electrici ty to all. The States are 
conscious of their primary responsibility of ensuring availability and distribution of electricity. 
The continued proactive initiatives of the Union Government in coordinated planning, 
supplementing generation through Central Public Sector Undertakings, inter-state and inter 
region transmission, rural electrification, providing financial assistance through various 
programmes and institutions, and in guiding the reforms process, along with the proactive 
stance of the States, are vital to achieve this  objective. 
3. The Conference acknowledges that the Bharat Nirman targets for rural electrification 
have to be met in order to ensure  mat rura l India has adequate access to electricity; and 
resolves that the Central Government would, through the Rajiv Gandhi Grameen Vidyutikaran 
Yojana,continue to assist the State Governments help expand their rural networks and 
extend household conn ections to BPL families as set out under Bharat Nirman. The 
Government of India, in discharge of its statutory functions under the Electricity Act, would 
extend all possible financial and techno-managerial support. The States would urgently 
formulate clear, cost effective and comprehe nsive rural electrification plans which would 
address the concerns of sustainability, availability, affordability and delivery of power. The 
States should also develop appropriate revenue and franchisee models that may use system 
improvements to meet the requirements of the rural areas and disadvantaged groups, 
particularly wherever it is a better alternativ e to existing arrangements. The Centre shall 
support the States in their commitment and ta ke into account the special requirements of 
different States. 
4. The Conference noted with concern that the country is presently facing serious peaking 
and energy shortages, and resolves that the States and the Centre would vigorously pursue 
the capacity addition programmes so as to create capacities in line with the rapid growth of 
demand of electricity and eliminate shortages within the 11th Plan to ensure the goal of 

Written Answers to (,10 MARCH, 2008] Unstarred Questions    175 
"Power for all by 2012." The Centre and the States would ensure timely placement of orders 
by December 2007 for all projects intended to give benefits during the 11th Plan and ensure 
regular monthly project monitoring for their timely commissioning along pre-determined 
milestones. The Centre would set up a National Power Project Management Board for 
monitoring the timely commissioning of the unprecedented capacity addition and associated 
transmission projects. The States would also set up similar dedicated apparatus. Immediate 
steps would also be taken to expedite the development of hydro power and renewable 
sources. The Centre would continue to ensure the timely development of inter-state and 
inter-region transmission lines, with active facilitation by the States. Matching sub-
transmission and distribution networks would be created by the States to synchronize with 
the capacity addition. The States supported the initiative of the Centre to set up Ultra Mega 
Power Projects (UMPPs). The Centre would also develop the, necessary transmission network 
for UMPPs. The States would continue to effect further improvement in the PLF of their 
existing generating stations. The Government of India would facilitate the timely and adequate 
availability of coal and gas for the generating plants at reasonable and competitive prices 
within the existing legal framework. The linkage from coal fields will be locationally rationalized, 
to the extent possible;. 
5. The Conference recognizes that an estimated captive generating capacity of about 
20,000 MW is being sub-optimally utilized in a phase of critical power shortage; and resolves 
that no generating capacity would be left idle. The States would facilitate captive power 
plants to provide spare generating capacity to the grid and strive to do away with restrictive 
levies, duties and regulations in a time-bound manner. 
6. The Conference further resolves that the States commit themselves to operationalizing 
'open access' in the transmission and distribution sectors and resolve to* issue policy directives 
to regulators, if necessary to appropriately restructure cross subsidy surcharge, wheeling 
charges and other charges, with a view to augment the quantum of power flowing into the 
grid in the prevailing environment of shortage. 
7. The Conference recognizes that the operationalizing of'open access' and competition 
in the supply of electricity to consumers would improve the supply position, help lower the 
tariffs and attract much needed investment in capacity addition; and resolved that the Centre 
and the States would unshackle generation, transmission and distribution to enhance the 
availability of electricity and its unhindered movement to consumers. The Centre and the 
States would also issue any n ecessary policy directives to any undertaking or regulator to 
this end, in the interest of consumers, within and outside the concerned State. 
8. The Conference recognizes that the current level of AT&C losses constitute a grave 
threat to the viability of the power sector and the distribution segment, which is currently 
losing about Rs.47,000 crores per annum, is the weakest link in the power system and 
resolves that the States commit themselves to achieve and sustain drastic reduction in the 
overall AT&C losses through the next five years, and at least to a level of 15% in the APDRP 
project areas as has been demonstrated by th e partiefpating stats in 163 towns and cities. 
Towards this end, the States with appropriate assistance from the Centre would establish the 
necessary baseline data and IT applications for energy accounting and auditing, besides 
ensuring a resolute elimination of electricity theft, which is negating various investments 

176    Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Unstarred Questions 
and initiatives for power sector reforms. It is further reiterated that where free or subsidized 
power is provided to a section of consumers, the State Government shall ensure upfront 
payment of the same to the utilities. 
9. The Conference recognizes that there is a very significant potential of saving electricity 
through its efficient use; and resolves that  Sates and the Centre should focus on Demand 
Side Management measures and ensure such interventions as would provide immediate 
results for saving electricity. These interven tions could include bulk procurement and 
distribution of CFLs, adoption of the Energy Conservation Building Code (ECBC), promoting 
and mandating the use of energy efficient pump sets and other energy efficient equipment 
and appliances, besides giving appropriate financial and tax incentives for their manufacture. 
10. To periodically review the implementation of the resolutions adopted in the Conference, 
it is decided to set up a Standing Group of Power Ministers under the Chairmanship of the 
Union Power Minister to meet once a quarter.

 t 1044. SHRI LALIT KISHORE CHATURVEDI: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether formation of companies by dissolving and dividing the State Electricity Boards 
into several parts has been profitable and the losses incurred by the Boards have come down; 
(b) if so, the details in that regard;

THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHILKUMAR SHINDE): (a) to (c) So, far 13 
States have reorganized their SEBs. Ten States namely Orissa, Haryana, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, 
Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Rajasthan, Delhi, Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh have done so under their 
respective State Electricity Reforms Acts. Assam, Maharashtra and West Bengal have 
reorganized their SEBs, under the provisions of the Electricity Act, 2003. Government of Tripura 
has corporatized its Electcirity Department. 
The Central Government had awarded a study to the Indian Institute of Public 
Administration (IIPA) on the impact of restructuring the State Electricity Boards. The broad 
conclusion of the study is that despite some shortcomings, the overall impact of restructuring has 
been positive and is in the right direction.

Commissions. The Power Finance Corporation (PFC), which lends funds to State Power 
utilities also, bring out an annual compilation on the results of financial performance of these 
utilities. Position of financial performance of utilities as compiled by PFC (State utility-wise 
including that of Rajasthan) for the years 2004-05, 2005-06 and 2006-07 is given in the 
enclosed Statement.

2006-07 were less than the losses in year 2004-05.

(i) Past dues of Central Public Sector Co mpanies against State Electricity Boards 
(SEBs) amounting to Rs. 34,957.96 crores had been securitised in the year 200\1. 
(ii) The Electricity Act, 2003 provides that the tariff determination is to be done by 
independent Electricity Regulatory Commissions. 
(iii) Section 65 of the Act provides that if the State Government requires the grant of 
any subsidy to any consumer or class of consumers in the tariff determined by the 
State Commissions, the State Government shall pay to the concerned utility/ 
licensee the amount required to compensate the grant of subsidy. 
(iv) The Accelerated Power Developmen t and Reforms Programme (APDRP) was 
launched in the year 2002-03 for assisting States in investment in strengthening 
of sub transmission and distribution syst ems for reducing technical losses and 
improving the quality of supply and also for incentivising through cash grants 
the reduction of cash losses by State Power Utilities. It is being proposed to 
continue APDRP during the Xlth Plan. 
(v) Legal provisions in Electricity Act, 2003 for dealing with theft of electricity have 
been further strengthened by the Electricity (Amendment) Act, 2007. 
(vi) Emphasis is given on metering of feeders and supply to consumers for energy 
accounting and auditing for identifying location of high losses.

Power savings 
t 1047. SHRI SATYAVRAT CHATURVEDI: 
SHRI MOTILAL VORA: 
MS.SUSHILATIRJYA: 
Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government has set a target of saving ten thousand megawatt of power 
during Eleventh Five Year Plan; 
(b) if so, the scheme being formulated for the same; 
(c) the percentage of power being lost in Transmission and Distribution (T&D) at present, 
and how much megawatt of power is lost due to this every year; 
(d) the steps being taken by Government to lessen the T&D losses; and 
(e) the scheme formulated by Government to check the theft of power from transmission 
lines? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHEL KUMAR SHINDE): (a) and (b) Yes, 
Sir. 8 new schemes have been formulated to promote power saving, which include-Bachat 
Lamp Yojana, Standard and Labelling Sc heme, Energy Conservation Building Code, 
Agricultural and Municipal Demand Side Management, Strengthening of Institutional 
Capacity of State Designated Agencies, En ergy Efficiency in Small and Medium 
Enterprises, Institutional strengthening of Bureau of Energy Efficiency and other energy 
efficiency institutions and contribution to the State Energy Conservation Fund. 
(c) Transmission and Distribution (T&D) losses for 2003-04,2004-05 and 2005-06 were 
32.53%, 31.25% and 30.42% respectively. For 2005-06, if the reasonable level of losses is 
taken as 15%, savings (15.42% of losses) in terms of installed generation capacity would be 
of the order of 14000 MW. 
(d) and (e) The Government has built a national consensus to focus on a time bound 
programme for reduction of Aggregate Technical and Commercial (AT&C) losses. Aresolution 
adopted in the Cheif Ministers' Conference held on 28.5.2007, inter-alia include, the 
commitment of the States for ensuring a resolute elimination of electricity theft. Accelerated 
Power Development & Reforms Programme (APDRP) was launched in 2002-03 to provide 
States for taking up technical, commercial and management measures to reduce the losses. 
Further Electricity Act, 2003 provides legal framework for making theft of electricity a cognizable 
offence. 
Load shedding in Delhi 
1048. SHRIMATI HEMAMALINI: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government is aware that the capital is experiencing rampant load shedding; 
(b) if so, whether Government has taken steps to mitigate the plight of consumers; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
t Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 

192    Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Unstarred Questions 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE): (a) to (d) During the 
current year (April, 2007 to January, 2008), Delhi faced marginal energy and peak shortage of 
0.4% and 1.1% respectively. 
Under Section 42 of the Electricity Act, 2003, it is the duty of a Distribution Licensee to 
develop and maintain an efficient, co-ordinated and economical distribution system in his 
area of supply and to supply electricity in accordance with the provisions contained in the 
Act. According to BSES Yamuna Power Limited (BYPL) and BSES Rajdhani Power Limited 
(BRPL), the supply in the licence area of BRPL and BYPL is quite stable, except that some 
interruptions for short durations are affected due to constraints such as under frequency/ 
low voltage and low availability of power etc. in the Northern Grid. Load shedding is resorted 
to during peak hours on the transformer/feeders having losses more than 50% to avoid 
burning of transformer and other equipments. 
According to North Delhi Power Ltd. (NDPL), there is no unscheduled power cut in NDPL 
area of supply due to inadequacy of distribution network capacity or equipment failure. Load 
shedding is done only under low frequency regime when there is gap between demand and 
supply in the Northern Grid and such load shedding is done strictly under specific instructions 
from DTL/Northern Grid. 
Electricity is a concurrent subject under the Constitution. The supply and distribution of 
electricity in a State/UT is within the purv iew of the respective State Government/State 
Power Utilities. The Government of India supplements the efforts of the State Government 
by establishing power plants in central sector through CPSUs etc.

Statement 
Detail of action to curb crimes against women and proposals for their empowerment 
Law and order and other criminal matters is a State subject under the Constitution and 
therefore the direct responsibility for dealing with enforcement of the concerned Acts is that 
of the State Governments and the mechanisms under them. The registration, investigation, 
detection and prevention of crimes against women is primarily the responsibility of the State 
Governments/UT Administrations. However, the Government of India has initited a number 
of measures to check such crimes, such as:—  
• Enacted the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 which provides 
for more effective protection of the Constitutional rights of women who are victims 
of violence of any kind occurring within the family including any unlawful demand 
for dowry. 
• setting up of help lines for women in distress under  the Swadhar Scheme. 
• support services to victims of violen ce through schemes such as Short Stay 
Homes and Swadhar under which shelter maintenance, counseling, capacity 
building, occupational training, medical aid and other services provided. 
• A scheme has been formulated on 13.11.2007 to change the mindset of the society 
towards the girl child and view her as an asset and not a burden namely, Conditional 
Cash Transfer with Insurance Cover Scheme" The scheme provides for cash 
transfers to family of the girl child (preferably the mother) on fulfilling certain 
conditionalities such as birth and registration of the girl child immunization, 
enrollment to school; retention in school, delaying the marriage age beyond 18 18 
years. Insurance cover is also proposed fo r the girl child as a safety net and to 
enable the girl to receive a lump sum at the age of 18 years. 
• launching of a comprehensive scheme under the name "Ujjawala" on 4.12.2007 for 
victims of trafficking and commercial sexual exploitation. The scheme has five 
components Prevention, Rescue, Rehabilitation, Re-integration and Repatriation. 
• redressal of grievances through interventions of National and State Commissions 
for Women. 
 organizing legal literacy and legal Awareness Camps. 
• implementation of schemes for (i) awareness generation and advocacy and (ii) 
economic empowerment of women through the programmes of Rashtriya Mahila 
Kosh, Swashakti Project, Swayamsidha Project, Swawlamban Programme and 
Support to Training & Employment Programme (STEP). 
• review of laws with a view to remove provisions which may be discriminatory to 
women and to enhance punishments for crimes against women. 
 sensitization of Judiciary and police and civil administration on gender issues. 
• follow up of reports of cases of atro cities against women received from varous 
sources, including NCW, with concerned authorities in the Central and the State 
Governments. 

Written Answers to [10 MARCH, 2008] Unstarred Questions    205 
Apart from legislative changes in the relevant Acts, instructions/guidelines have been 
issued to the State Governments/Union Territo ry Administrations to effectively enforce 
legislation relating to crimes against women and monitor the enforcement and to give more 
focused attention to improving the administration of criminal justice system and to take such 
measures as are necessary for the prevention of crime against women and other vulnerable 
sections of society. The measures suggested include: 
• sensitizing of police officials charged with the responsibility of protecting the 
women. 
• vigorously enforce the existing legislation relating to dowry violence. 
• set up women police cells in police stations and exclusive women police stations. 
• provide institutional support to the victims of violence. 
• provide counseling to victims of rape. 
• take measures to eliminate trafficking in women. States have also been advised to 
constitute State Advisory Committees to advise on trafficking matters. 
• ensure wider recruitment of women police officers. 
• train police personnel in special lawas dealing with atrocities against women. 
• setting up of Fast Track Courts. 
• seting up of Family Courts. 
• appointment of Dowry Prohibition Officers and notification of Rules under the 
Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961.

Written Answers to [10 MARCH, 2008] Unstarred Questions   207 
Statement 
Main points of the recommendations made by NCW 
The National Commission for Women has made the following main recommendations:— 
(i) The words in connection with the marriage of said parties occurring in section 2 of 
the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 relating to the definition of dowry, may be deleted. 
(ii) A penalty of imprisonment of not less than 3 years and fine of not less than Rs. 
15,000/- may be introduced for the parents/relatives of the bride or bridegroom for 
non-maintenance of lists of presents under the Dowry Prohibition (Maintenance of 
Lists of Presents to the Bride and Bridegroom) Rules, 1985. 
(iii) The penalty laid down in the said Act for giving dowry may be reduced to 
imprisonment of not less than one year and fine of not less than Rs. 15,000/-
unless the person can prove that he was compelled to give dowry. 
(iv) Amend section 6 of the said Act (dowry to be for the benefit of the wife or her 
heirs) in order to provide that in the event of the death of any woman, whether 
due to natural causes or otherwise, whether within 7 years or after 7 years of her 
marriage, any property to which she is entitled under the section will be transferred 
to her children or to her parents if she has no children, and not to her heirs. 
(v) Empower the Service Provider or the Protection Officer functioning under the 
Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, under section 7 of the 
Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, to lodge a complaint of commission of an offence. 
(vi) The words 'soon before her death' occurring in sub-section (1) of section 304B 
IPC (Dowry death) may be replaced by the words anytime before her death' and 
any death occurring in the circumstances mentioned in the sub-section even after 
7 years of marriage should be considered as dowry death. The minimum 
punishment laid down in sub-section (2) of section 304B IPC should be raised 
from 7 years to 10 years and death may be prescribed as the maximum penalty 
alternate to the existing penalty of imprisonment for life.
