Health hazard of tobacco 
* 122. DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANIA: 
SHRI LALIT KISHORE CHATURVEDI: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) the dimension/statistics pertaining to health hazard by tobacco; 
(b) how many tobacco-related deaths occur in the country daily/annually; 
(c) whether 40 per cent of all health problems in the country are due to tobacco and the 
Centre is spending Rs. 45 crores thereof; 
(d) whether a powerful lobby is opposing ware against tobacco; 
(e) what measures are being taken to effectively enforce total ban on smoking in public; 
and 
(f) how hazardous is 'GUTKA' and what is his Ministry's stand regarding its ban? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): 
(a) to (c) There are studies to indicate that approximately 40% of the diseases burden in the 
country is associated with some form of tobacco and its products. Approximately 50% of all 
cancer deaths in the country are due to tobacco consumption. The majority of the cardio 
vascular diseases, cancer and lung disorders are directly attributable to tobacco consumption. 
No such specific data regarding the death due to tobacco year wise is being maintained 
centrally. However as per report of the Tobacco Control of India 2004, every year approximately 
0.8 million people die due to tobacco related illn ess in India. As per an article titled 'A 
Nationally Representative Case—Control Study of Smoking and Death in India published 
by New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM) dated 13th February, 2008, smoking causes a 
large number of premature deaths in India. This study estimates that in 2010, approximately 
1 million premature deaths would occur due to smoking tobacco in some form or other. Of the 
1 million deaths, approximately 70% (1 lakh women and 6 lakh men) will occur in middle age 
rather than old age. 
(d) Insofar as lobby opposing the Tobacco Control efforts, there have been various 
representations from industry and other relevant stakeholder objecting to the specific Rules/ 
Provision of the Act, 2003. The Government has taken into consideration these 
representations, while formulating the policies keeping in mind the overall public health 
objective. 
(e) Government has enacted a comprehensive tobacco control legislation titled "The 
Cigarettes And Other Tobacco Products (Prohibition of Advertisements and Regulation to 
Trade And Commerce, Production, Supply and Distribution) Act, 2003, in May 2003, for 
discouraging the use of cigarettes and other tobacco products. Some important provisions 
of the Act, which are applicable to whole of the country, are:— 
 
• Prohibition of direct and indirect advertisement of all tobacco products. 
• Prohibition of smoking in a public place; 
• Prohibition of sale of all tobacco products to a person below the age of 18 years 
and within a radius of 100 yards of educational institutions. 
• Mandatory depiction of statutory health warning on all tobacco packs.

Governments/UTs are the implementing agenci es for enforcing these provisions. Central

crores has been proposed in the Eleventh five-year plan. For 2007-08, Rs. 40.00 crores was 
allocated under the National Tobacco Control Programme.   . 
(f) Gutka is a tobacco product which is injurious to health. At present there is no proposal

Promotion of agricultural research 
*134. DR.ABHISHEK MANU SINGHVI: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be 
pleased to state what steps are being taken by Government to promote agricultural research 
in the country and what is the fund allocation for such research and how much of this is 
spent on promoting young agricultural scientists? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHR1SHARAD PAWAR): Agricultural Research in the 
country is being promoted through National Agricultural Research System (NARS), which is 
composed of 42 State Agricultural Universities (SAUs) and one Centra) Agricultural University 
and 95 Research Institutes. In addition, 61 All India Coordinated Research Projects and 16 
Network Programmes area also in operation. These centres primarily address research in the 
field of Crop Science, Horticulture, Na tural Resource Management, Agricultural , 
Engineering. Animal Science, Fisheries and Extension. There are also 558 multidisciplinary 
centres called Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVKs) for assessment, refinement and demonstration 
of frontline technologies. 
The focus of research programmes is to meet food and nutritional security of the country-
as well as making Indian agriculture globally competitive both cost and quality-wise, raising 
farm income thus improving quality of life of farmers, facilitating flow of knowledge and 
technology to farmers, and promoting sustainable use of our natural resources. 
National Agricultural Innovation Project with the support of World Bank is also in operation with 
main objective to facilitate accelerated and sustainable transformation of Indian      agriculture 
for enhancing productivity, profitability and livelihood security. 
The fund allocated for research during 2008-09 is tentatively Rs. 1760 crore while it was 
Rs. 1620 crore during 2007-08. The Xlth Plan fund allocation of DARE/ICAR is Rs. 12,023 
* crore against Rs. 5,368 crore during Xth Five Year Plan. The young scientists are encouraged 
to avail various scholarships/fellowships, study leave/sabbatical leave to continuously 
' enhance their skills through specialized trainings. The budget allocation for research is made 
on the basis of schemes/projects as per their actual requirement and not on the basis of 
young or other scientists basis. However, in order to lay emphasis on getting good young 
scientists, the Department is funding all SAUs  through its major scheme of Strengthening 
and Development of SAUs including scheme of establishing a Centre of Excellence in Niche 
area in each of the SAUs. The budget allocation for this scheme during 2007-08 was Rs. 310 
crore while tentative allocation during 2008-09 is Rs. 347 crore.

Amendment in Human Organ Transplantation Act 
* 138. SHR1 SHANTARAM LAXMAN NAIK: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government proposes to introduce any amendment in the existing law to provide 
for more stringent punishment for illegal kidney transplant; 
(b) the details of the proposed amendment, if any; 
(c) whether the proposed bill to regulate clinical establishments which is presently before the 
Standing Committee would also deal with the matter; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBUMANI RAMADOSS): (a) 
and (b) Yes, Sir. The Honorable High court of Delhi in CWP No. 813/2004 vide its order dated 
06.09.2004 had set up a Committee to examine the provisions of Tansplantation of Human 
Organs Act, 1994, and the Transplantation of Human Organs Rules, 1995. The report was submitted 
on 25.05.2005. A National Consultation was held on 18.05.2007 and the report was submitted in the 
second fortnight of August, 2007. The recomm ended changes required amendment in the 
Transplantation of Human Organs Act, 1994 and the Rules framed thereunder. These changes are 
intended to facilitate genuine cases, increase transparency in transplantation procedures and to 
provide deterrent penalties for violation of the law. In so far as the Act is concerned, the 
following amendments have been proposed: 
(0 to empower Union Territories, specially Government of NCT of Delhi to have their own 
appropriate authority instead of DGHS and/or Additonal DG (Hospitals). 
(ii) To make the punishments under the Act harsh and cognizable for the illegal 
transplantation activities to deter the offenders from committing this crime. 
(iii) To provide for registration of the centres for removal of organs from the cadavers and 
brain stem dead patients for harvesting of organs instead of registration of centres for 
transplantations only. 
(iv) To allow swap operations between the related donor and recipients who do not match 
themselves but match with other similar donors/recipients. 
Sale/purchase of human organs is already prohibited under Transplantation of Human Organs 
Act, 1994. Appropriate authorities established under this Act are responsible and empowered to 
check the illegal activities of human organs trafficking. 
(c) and (d) A Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Bill 2007 has been 
introduced in Lok Sabha on 30.08.2007. The Bill seeks to provide for registration and regulation

clinical establishments in the country. National Council for clinical establishments has 
been set up to determine the standards for clinical establishments, classify the clinical 
establishment into different categories, develop minimum standards and their periodic review, 
compile, maintain and update a national register of clinical establishments, perform any other 
function determined by the Central Government, from time to time.

783. SHRI C. PERUMAL: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state:

failed to check manufacturing, distribution and use of spurious and sub-standard pesticides

country had failed to check manufacturing, distribution and use of spurious and sub-
standard pesticides which has caused huge lo ss to farmers. The Government regulates the 
manufacture and use of pesticides under the provisons of the Insecticides Act, 1968. The 
Registration Committee, constituted under Section 5 of the Insecticides Act, 1968, registers 
pesticides only after having satisfied itself of their efficacy and safety. Quality assurances of 
pesticides is ensured by the State Government through regular drawl and analysis of pesticides 
samples through a network of Insecticide Inspectors, Insecticide Analysts and Pesticides 
Testing Laboratories. Under the provisons of the Act penal action is taken by the States 
against manufacturers of spurious and substandard pesticides.

strengthening of Pesticides Testing Laboratories. The Government also promotes judicious 
use of pesticides through its policy of Integrated Pest Management (IPM).

BHURIA): (a) The Central Government has requested State Governments by circulating a 
Model Agricultural Produce Marketing (Regulation) Act and the Model Rules thereunder, 
for making provisions to facilitate contract fanning which envisages cultivation of specified 
crops by the farmers under an agreement for a sponsoring agency so that the produce could 
be sold to the sponsoring agency at a pre-decided price. Under this arrangement, the Central

(b) The contract farming arrangements are quite helpful to the farmers in securing better 
remuneration for their produce, as such arrangements cover the price risk and also the production 
risk to a great extent. Contract Farming has the potential of combining farmers' efficiency with 
economy of scale, utilizing corporate management skills, providing assured markets and reducing 
transaction costs in the value chain by ensuring vertical integration. Such tie-ups have special 
significance for small and marginal farmers, who have small marketed surplus and do not have 
staying power. They may not individually be capable of investing in technology, but through self 
help groups or cooperatives, there could emerge a desirable institutional framework, through 
which farmers can suitably reap the benefits of contract farming arrangements. Contract farming 
arrangements are prevalent for the cultivation of foodgrains crops also and as such, it is not

792. SHR1 EKANATH K. THAKUR: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that even though India possesses the world's second largest 
cultivable land area (147 million hectares) after the US, India is fast decimating this asset by 
failing to salvage its abysmal agricultural productivity, which is very low in comparison even 
with other emerging economies like China, Thailand and Brazil; 

Written Answers to [10 MARCH, 2008] Starred and Unstarred   253 
Questions of7th March, 2008 
(b) whether it is also a fact that average cereal yield in 2005 was only 2,000 kg. per hectare in 
India as compared to over 6,000 kg. in the US and 5,000 kg.in China; and 
(c) if so, the steps Government proposes to take to boost the agricultural productivity? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI KANTILAL 
BHURIA): (a) and (b) As per information available at Food and Agriculture Organization's (FAO) 
internet site 'http://faostat.fao.org' the arable land of India in 2005 was 159.65 million hectare as 
against 174.45 million hectare in USA. The average yield of cereals in 2005 in China, 
Thailand, Brazil and USA was 5229 Kg./hectare, 3012 Kg/hectare, 2883 Kg./Hectare and 6373 
Kg./hectare respectively as against India's average yield of 2451 Kg./hectare. 
(c) Several programmes have been taken up to boost agricultural productivity. These include, 
Macro Management of Agriculture providing flexibility to the States to take up suitable projects 
and setting up of National Rainfed areas Authority. In addition, the National Food Security Mission 
has been taken up to increase foodgrains production by 20 million tonnes by the end of the 
Eleventh Plan. Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana has also been launched to incentivise the States to 
invest more in agriculture sector. 
Area sown under oilseed in kharif season 
793. SHRI D. RAJA: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is fact that the area sown under kharif oilseed crop for the new season is 
16.47 million hectares as against 14.88 hectares in the previous year; 
(b) if so, what are the prime reasons for this expanded area under oilseed cultivation in the current 
season; 
(c) what will be the expected production of oilseed this year; and 
(d) whether Government hopes to create self-sufficiency in oil seed by 2009-10; and the 
details of the steps proposed by Government to increase oilseed production on a sustained 
basis? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI KANTI LAL 
BHURIA): (a) and (b) As per the 2nd Advance Estimates, the area sown under Kharif oilseed crops 
is estimated at 17.71 million hectares during 2007-08 as against 16.77 lakh hectares in the 
previous year. The area coverage during 2007-08 increased because of favourable weather 
conditions at the time of sowing. 
(c) During 2007-08, the production of oilseeds is estimated at 27.16 millions tonnes (2nd 
Advance Estimates released on 7th February, 2008) comprising 17.57 million tonnes in Kharif 
season and 9.59 million tonnes in Rabi season. 
(d) The demand-supply in oilseeds is met through the import of edible oils. To increase the 
production of oilseeds and make the country self-sufficient, the Government is 
implementing a Centrally sponsored "Integrated Schemes of Oilseeds, Pulses, Oil Palm and 
Maize (ISOPOM)" in 14 major oilseeds growing States in the country. Under the Scheme, 
financial assistance is provided for purchase of breeder seeds, production of foundation and 
certified seeds, distribution of seed minikits, distribution of plant protection chemicals and 
equipments, weedicides, distribution of sprinkler sets, water carrying pipes and training to 
encourage fanners to grow these crops.

Justifiable prices for agricultural produce 
t 796. SHRI PYARELAL KHANDELWAL: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that how to get farmers justifiable prices for their produce, is not a 
matter of priority for Government; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that despite all Government announcements/packages farmer 
suicides continue unabated; and 
(c) if not, the details of efforts and achievements made by Government in getting farmers 
lucrative price for their produce? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI KANTI 
LAL BHURIA): (a) to (c) The Government's price policy for agricultural commodities 
seeks to ensure remunerative prices to the farmers for their produce with a view to 
encourage higher investment and production, and to safeguard the interest of consumers 
by making available supplies at reasonable prices. The price policy also seeks to evolve 
a balanced and integrated price structure in the perspective of the overall needs of the 
economy. 
The Government decides on the Minimum Support Price (MSP) for various agricultural 
commodities taking into account the recommendations of the Commission for Agricultural Costs 
and Prices (CACP), the views of State Governments and Central Ministries as well as such other 
relevant factors which are considered important for fixation of support prices.  The CACP, 
while formulating its recommendations on price policy considers a number of important 
factors which includes cost of production. 
The causes for suicide by farmers, as reported by the State Governments, are broadly 
*    crop failure, indebtendness, drought, social and economic insecurity. The Government 
being sensitive to the difficulties of the farming community, the Union Budget for 2008-09

       (b) if  so, the details thereof; and

has become unremunerative to them following increase in the prices of inputs and element of

the farmers for the agricultural produce? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI KANTILAL 
BHURIA): (a) There is no survey specifically undertaken by Government of India to analyze 
the causes that led to suicide by farmers. However, the State Governments have broadly 
reported crop failure, indebtedness, drought, social and economic insecurity as causes for

(b) and (c) The Government's price policy for agricultural commodities seeks to ensure 
remunerative prices to the grow ers for their produce with a view to encourage  higher 
investment and production, and to safeguard the interest of consumers by making available 
supplies at reasonable prices. The price policy also seeks to evolve a balanced and integrated 
prices structure in the perspective of the overall needs of the economy. Towards this end,

agencies. The designated central nodal agencies are required to intervene in the market for

802. DR.V. MAITRE YAN: 
SHRI AMAR SINGH:

in the country, State-wise;

Questions of 7th March, 2008 
(c) the steps being taken to protect the crops during these severe weather conditions in 
the country; 
(d) whether any relief programme is being considered by Government to compensate the 
losses to the affected farmers due to these weather calamities; and 
*  (e) if so, the details thereof?  
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI KANTILAL   
BHURIA): (a) and (b) Due to severe cold condition prevailing in the country, standing rabi 
crops have been damaged in the States of Punjab, Haryana, Jammu and Kashmir, Rajasthan, 
Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh. The Punjab  State held reported severe loss to the 
Horticultural Crops and nominal loss to the Agriculture. The State of Haryana has reported 
loss to crop of mustard to the extent of 223000 tonnes with value of Rs. 401.56 crores, gram 
at 600 tonnes with a value of Rs. 0.98 crores. The State of Jammu and Kashmir reported the 
loss to the extent of Rs. 45.10 crore to the crops of wheat, oilseed vegetables, potatoes and

and Tara Mira crops. The Madhya Pradesh State reported the damage to the crop of gram, 
lentil and Arhar to the extent of 015 lakh ha. and the State of Uttar Pradesh has reported the 
damage to the tune of 11 % in mustard, 5% in wheat, 7% in barley and 22% in gram/peas/lentil

damaged tips of branches or shoot, burn leave/waste material in the orchard to create smock

(d) and (e) Cold wave frost is not covered under the guidelines of Calamity Relief Fund 
(CRF) and National Calamity Contingency Fund (NCCF). However, the farmers are entitled 
for compensation under the National Agricultural Insurance Scheme (NAIS) implemented 
through the State Governments.

part of the control and containment operations against bird flu in the State. Further, another 
3.03 lakh poultry birds have been culled as part of preventive culling undertaken in the 
border areas of Assam, Bihar and Jharkhand and West Bengal. 
(c) Bird flu can, in addition to poultry, also affect wild/migratory birds. 
(d) The Government of India has drawn up an 'Action Plan of Animal Husbandry for 
Preparednes, Control and Containment of Avian Influenza' and circulated the same to all 
States/Union Territories for compliance. The preventive steps against future occurrence of 
such diseases include maintaining strict surveillance, prompt reporting of any unusual 
mortality of livestock and birds,drawing regular samples, capacity building in laboratory 
diagnostic facilities, strengthening of anim al quarantine stations and creating overall 
awareness on bio-security in livestock production system.

The Government has taken a series of measures to streamline TPDS. Earlier Programme 
Evaluation Organization (PEO) of Planning Commission and ORG MARG New Delhi, evaluated 
the Targeted Public Distribution System and submitted their reports in 2005. These studies 
reported diversion of foodgrins, exclusion and inclusion errors in identification of BPL families 
and non-viability of functioning of Fair Price shops. 
Based on findings of these studies, a Ni ne Point Action Plan is already under 
implementation by State and UT Governments for stengthening of TPDS. A copy of the 
said Action Plan is enclosed at Statement I (See below). Its implementation is monitored by 
the Central Government. Implementation of nine point action plan by State and UT 
Governments has led to deletion of about 65 lakh bogus/ineligible ration cards by 11 
States/UT while reviewing the lists of their existing BPL/AAY households. Instructions 
have been issued to all the States/UTs take  action against persons found in possession of 
bogus or fake ration cards and Government staff found responsible for issuing ration 
cards to ineligible persons. 
Additionally, a revise Citizens' Charter ha s been issued recently for adoption and 
implementation by State/UTs Governments for facilitating use by citizens of provisions of 
Right to Information (RTI) Act, 2005 in relation to functioning of TPDS. 
Furthermore, to ensure that TPDS foodgrains reach the targeted families and to minimize 
scope for their diversion, APL allocations have been rationalized. Concurrent evaluation of 
TPDS has been taken up. Training Programm es for TPDS functionaries and Awareness 
campaign for TPDS beneficiaries are being taken up. Computerization of TOPS has been 
initiated. Use of new technologies such as Global Positioning system is being piloted. Revised 
policy on distribution of wheat flour has been issued. 
Statement 
Action plan for strengthening of TPDS 
(i) Continuous review of the BPL and AAY lists to eliminate bogus ration cards and 
to ensure coverage of only eligible BPL and Antyodaya families. 
(ii) Ensuring leakage-free and diversion-free distribution of PDS commodities, regular 
inspection by different levels of functionaries, strict action against guilty persons/ 
agencies. 
(iii) Involvement of Panchayati Raj Institutions in PDS operations-PRI 
representatives on Advisory Committee, running of fair price shops by 
Panchayats and effective representation of Panchayati Raj representatives on 
vigilance Committees. 
(iv) Ensuring transparency in working of PDS, display of BPL and AAY lists by fair 
price shops, observance of notified timings by fair price shops. 
(v) Use of Information Technology, computerization of TPDS operations, display of 
fair price shop-wise and district wise allocations of PDS commodities on web-
sites for public scrutiny. 
(vi) Carryout door-step delivery of PDS commodities to fair price shops.

Ensuring timely availability of and issuance of foodgrains by fair price shops. 
(viii) Creating awareness among public about PDS operations training Vigilance 
Committees of intricacies of PDS operations. 
(ix) Making fair price shops financially viable entities-allowing them to sell non PDS 
items etc.

Rise in prices of essential commodities 
826. SHRI RAM DAS AGARWAL: Will the Minister of CONSUMER AFFAIRS, 
FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government has conducted any study of day-to-day rising prices of the 
consumer goods during the years 2006-07,2007-08, till February 2008 like vegetables, pulses, 
rice, edible oil, wheat, etc.; 
(b) what are Government's plans to check the rising trend of price rise of these commodities; 
(c) the details of import of rice, wheat, pulses, edible oil, etc. during 2006-07, 2007-08 
indicating the import-price of these items and qunatities thereof, year-wise; and 
(d) the future position of agriculture products and whether Government is expecting any 
shortfall? 

292    Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Starred and Unstarred 
Questions of 7th March, 2008 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD 
AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI TASLIMUDDIN): (a) No study has been conducted 
by the Government. However retail prices of essential commodities are being monitored 
by this department on day to day basis. It has been observed that the retail prices of 
gram dal.sugar, potato and onion are now showing a declining trend. Retail prices of 
wheat, which was steady at Rs. 12 per kg for the last one year, has now shown a marginal 
increase of Rs. 1 per kg since mid of January 2008. Retail prices of gram dal which 
reached to peak level of Rs. 42.50 per kg during September, 2006 now reduced to Rs. 34 
per kg. Retail prices of potato, which reached to peak level of Rs. 17 per kg during 
October, 2006, now reduced to Rs.8 per kg.Retail prices of onion which reached to peak 
level of Rs. 23 per kg during September, 2007 now reduced to Rs.8 per kg. Retail prices of 
tur dal have stabilized at Rs. 41 per kg Retail prices of ground nut oil and vanaspati oil 
has been stabilized at Rs. 121 per kg and Rs. 68 per kg since mid of October 2007 and 
December 2007 respectively. Retail prices of mustard oil show an upward trend during 
current year and are currently Rs. 70 per kg at Delhi, due to crop damage by cold waves 
in Rajasthan and other States. Retail prices of Rice, which was earlier showing steady 
trend at Rs. 15 per kg since the beginning of current year, is now showing an increasing 
trend since December, 2007 and is now Rs. 18 per kg mainly owing to a hike in MSP and 
bonus. 
(b) Government monitors price movement of essential commodities such as wheat, rice, 
pulses & edible oil at the highest level and has responded by taking a series of measures 
such as augmenting domestic supplies of wheat, edible oil and pulses through imports at 
reduced rates of duty and ban on exports of pulses and wheat. Exports of onion are controlled 
by using appropriate minimum export prices. As a measure of abundant precaution futures 
trading in wheat, rice tur and urad has been suspended. State Governments are introduce 
and enforce stock-limits.

(a) whether consumer protection courts/forums have been established at the State level 
and district level; 
(b) whether Government provide any assist ance to the State Governments for the 
establishment of above courts/forums; 
(c) if so, the funds allocated during the last three years for this purpose, State-wise;

cases? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND 
PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI TASLIMUDDIN): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) No, Sir. The establishment of State Commi ssions and District Fora and providing 
infrastructural facilities, manpower etc. for their effective functioning is the responsibility of 
the State Governments/UTs. However, in or der to supplement the efforts of the State 
Governments, the Central Government provided a One-Time financial assistance for 
strengthening infrastructural facilities of Consumer Fora to the extent of Rs. 61.80 crore 
during 1995-96 & Rs. 10.20 crore during 2004-05 to the States/UTs. Under the scheme of 
"Integrated Project on Consumer Protection", additional financial assistance of Rs. 40.32 
crore has been extended to States during 2006-07 to meet the gap in in frastructure of Consumer 
Fora. A further sum of Rs. 24.31 crore has been released to States so far under this scheme 
during the current financial year.

828.SHRIMATI MOHSINA KIDWAI: Will the Minister  of CONSUMER AFFAIRS, 
FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that 40 per cent of the ration cards meant for the below poverty line 
are being held by people who are not poor, 
(b) whether it is also a fact that as per study in Uttar Pradesh alone there are 11 million 
ration cards and same thing is with so many other States; 

Written Answers to [10 MARCH, 2008] Starred and Unstarred   299 
Questions of 7th March, 2008 
(c) if so, what Government has done to weed out bogus ration cards in the PDS and take 
action against the people who are involved in the racket; 
(d) how many such cases have been identified during the last one year and the action 
taken thereon; 
 
(e) whether Government has evaluated the performance of targeted PDS to know whether 
it reaches the targeted people; and 
(f) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND 
PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (DR. AKHILESH PRASAD SINGH): (a) to (d) National Council for 
Applied Economic Research (NCAER) conducted a concurrent evaluation of TPDS during 
the 2006-07 in six states namely Assam, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Rajasthan, Mizoram and Uttar 
Pradesh. NCAER in their report has mentioned that in case of AAY card holders, PDS food 
was being distributed quite satisfactory. In the case of BPL, almost all the six states had 
incidence od diversion. A statement-I showing the number of BPL Householders in 2000 as 
accepted bt Government of India & BPL ration cards issued by States & UT Governments as 
reported by 31.10.2008 is enclosed. (See below) 
Through consultation with State/UT Governments, a nine-point action plan was evolved 
during 2006 for strengthening of TPDS, and curbing leakages and diversion, which is under

Recommendations of Wadhwa Committee 
834. SHRID. RAJA: Will the Minister of CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government has a proposal under consideration to overhaul the present 
Public Distribution System (PDS) in the country on the basis of the Wadhwa Committee 
recommendations; and 
(b) if so, the main recommendations of the Wadhwa Committee and what measures are 
being taken to revjew the present PDS? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND 
PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (DR. AKHILESH PRASAD SINGH): (a) and (b) Central Vigilance 
Committe(CVC) with Justice D.P. Wadhwa as Chairman was set up by the Supreme Court to 
look into maladies affecting functioning of Public Distribution System (PDS) and to suggest 
remedial measures. The Supreme Court's direction to CVC was to conduct this study initially 
for the TPDS in Delhi, to be followed up on all India basis. The Committee has submitted 
its report on TPDS in Delhi in August, 2007 to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court in 
its order dated 10.01.2008 has ordered that similar exercise be undertaken by the CVC for 
the entire country and thereafter the Supreme Court would consider the suggestions of the 
CVC and shortfalls noticed. Thus the report submitted by CVC so far is only for TPDS in 
Delhi and does not cover other States. Acopy of summery of recommendations of CVC is 
given at the Statement (See below). 
Since the report of CVC submitted so far is for TPDS in Delhi, regarding recommendation 
of CVC to abolish APL category or limit APL coverage to households having annual income 
of rupees less than one lakh, Government of Delhi has taken a decision in principle to limit 
distribution of Specified Food Articles (SFAs) to only those APL card holders, who have 
their annual family income of less then Rs\ 1 lakh or are not Income Tax payees. 
The Central Government has also taken into consideration one suggestion of the CVC 
to distribute wheat flour to BPL families under TPDS while issuing the revised policy on the 
subject on 17.01.2008. 
Based on earlier evaluation reports, 9-point action plan is under implementation to 
strengthen TPDS. The TPDS is also being got evaluated concurrently through NCAER and 
IIPA. 
To facilitate use of Right to Information provisions, a revised Citizens' Charter has been 
issued in July, 2007 for States and UT Governments to implement. 
In addition, awareness campaign traini ng programmes for TPDS functionaries, 
computerization of TPDS and piloting of new technologies like global postioning system, 
stemping of bags containing TPDS foodgrains, are being taken up to improve functioning of 
the TPDS. 
Statement 
Sum and Substance of the Recommendations 
(i) Abolishing the APL category and raising the income criteria of BPL up to annual 
income of Rs. 49,244/- as most of th e foodgrain allocated for APL category is 
diverted in as much as by and large it is not lifted by persons belonging to the APL 
category. There is every likelihood of outcry against abolition of the APL category

Questions of 7th March, 2008 
by F.P.S. dealers and protests by vested  groups and hence if the Court is of the 
view that it may not be possible or desirable to abolish the APL category altogether, 
it may consider limiting the APL category to households whose annual income is 
Rs. one lakh. 
(ii) Immediate identification of BPL and AAY families — to check exclusion of poor 
households. 
(iii) Elimination of bogus/fake cards by means of a door-to-door to survey by a reputed 
agency-also collection of data for computerization. 
(iv) Zero tolerance-strengthening of the Enforcement Wing and Anti Hoarding Cell 
and making public servants engaged in PDS accountable-establishing flying squads 
to inspect the movement and distribution of food grains. Whenever a FPS is 
sealed because of some malpractic, its  licence be straigth-away suspsended/ 
revoked, Ration Card holders attached to  that FPS could be transferred to the 
nearby FPS or mobile van to be put in service or a Kirana shop of the area already 
selected, could be entrusted temporarily to distribute PDS foodgrains. 
(v) Computerization-use of technology—computerization of the activity providing 
an end-to-end automated system involving minimum human intervention. This 
would involve automation of the interface between the FPS and the consumer on 
one hand and the FPS and the FSO on the other so as to make the functioning of 
the FPS's transparent. 
(vi) Establishment of a Helpline. 
(vii) E-banking — amounts towards transport charges and cost of foodgrains should 
be remitted by FPS by ECS instead of by way of bank draft and handing over to 
the Circle Inspector etc., thus avoiding paper work. 
(viii) Distribution of wheat flour on option basis instead of wheat to BPL households— 
strict provision to put in place to check that good quality of wheat meant for PDS 
is not replaced by sub-sta ndard wheat by fiourmills et c.—general instructions 
could be given to sell only the fortified 'atta' with essential nutrients before 
selling in the open marketing/PDS—this is to make the implementation easier in all 
respects and also for avoiding diversion and leakage. 
(ix) Ombudsman/Regulator—independent agency to be created to monitor the working 
of the PDS—existing system is inactive and ineffective and corrupt.  
(x) Functions of the Delhi State Civil Supplies Corporation (DSCSC) to be taken over 
by the Department of Food and Civil Supplies—there is no Vigilance machinery 
or enforcement agency with the DSCSC to check diversion of food grains by the 
trucks engaged by the DSCSC—large scale diversion of foodgrains by these 
trucks. 
(xi) Food coupons—to begin with to be tried on a pilot basis in any two circles.  
(xii) Constitution and strengthening of Vigilance Committees at State/District Levels. 
(xiii) Strengthening the legal regime. 
•   (xiv) Streamlining the system of allotment of FPS licenses and steps for provision of 
reasonable commission to the FPS owners. 
(xv) Public awareness campaigns to be carried out to increase awareness among the

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND 
PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI TASLIMUDDIN): (a) and (b) Increase in domestic price rise 
has been mainly due to inflation in some food articles mainly rice, tur dal and edible oils 
witnessed globally due to inadequate supplies in relation to demand, diversion of food 
grains to bio-fuel and animal feed and, production losses due to inclement weather conditions. 
Some Increase in prices of some food articles such as rice and pulses in the country is also 
on account of hike in Minimum Support Price (MSP), bonus and decline in domestic 
production. Government is closely monitoring movement in prices of essential commodities 
such as wheat, pulses & edible oil and has responded by taking a series of measures such as 
(i) augmentation of availability of wheat through imports and banning export of wheat; 
(ii) protecting vulnerable sections of society through Targeted Public Distribution System 
(TPDS) and Antodaya Anna Yojana (AAY); (iii) reduction in Customs duty on import of 
pulses to zero; (iv) banning export of pulses;  (v) initiating imports of pulses through the 
State agencies such as NAFED, PEC Ltd., MMT C and STC; (vi) directing Public Sector 
Undertakings (PSUs) to import edible oils and to augment edible oils availability in the 
domestic market; (vii) reducing import duty on crude sunflower oil, crude palm oil (CPO) and 
Soya oils; (viii) as a matter of abundant caution, delisted all contracts of wheat, rice, tur and 
urad from commodity futures Exchanges. 
(c) and (d) As per the GDP estimates at constant prices (base 1999-2000) released by the 
Central Statistical Organisation (CSO), the growth rate in GDP of trade sector as a whole has 
been estimated at 8.1 % during the year 2005-06. Separate official estimates of rate growth of 
the share of retail sector and organized retail in GDP are not available. No studies have been 
conducted by the Government to assess whethe r the increase in organized retail trading 
added momentum to the price rise.

838.   SHRI SITARAM YECHURY: 
SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: 
SHRI MAT1 SUPRTYA SULE: 
Will the Minister of CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be

(b) if so, the reason therefor and the details thereof in comparison to the price of essential 
commodities from May, 2004 to January, 2008; 
(c) the steps initiated by Government to control the price rise and also to affect the impact 
of price on consumers; 
(d) whether Government is considering to strengthen the PDS system and expand it in the 
view of steep price hike; and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND 
PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI TASLIMUDDIN): (a) There has been no continuous increase 
in Prices of essential commodities. While comparing the prices of essential commodities from 
May, 2004 to January, 2008 for 4 Metros, it has been observed that retail prices of sugar had 

Written Answers to [10 MARCH, 2008] Starred and Unstarred   313 
Questions of 7th March, 2008 been 
declining from mid 2006, and after a brief spurt in mid 2007 they again declined. Retail prices 
of gram dal, sugar, potato and onion are also showing a declining trend. In Delhi, retail prices 
of wheat, which was steady at Rs. 12 per kg for the last one year, has now shown a marginal 
increase of Rs. 1 per kg since mid of January 2008. Retail prices of gram dal which reached to 
peak level of Rs. 42.50 per kg during September 2006 have now declined to Rs. 34 per kg. 
Retail prices of potato, which reached to peak level of Rs. 17 per kg during October 2006, 
are now quoted at Rs. 8 per kg. Retail prices of onion which reached to peak level of Rs. 23 per 
kg during September 2007 have declined to Rs. 8 per kg. Retail prices of tur dal have 
stabilized at Rs. 41 per kg. Retail prices of ground nut oil and vanaspati oil has been stabilized 
at Rs. 121 per kg and Rs. 68 per kg since mid of October 2007 and December 2007 respectively. 
Only retail prices of mustard oil show an upward trend during 2007 and are currently Rs. 69 
per kg, mainly due to reports of crop damage by cold waves in Rajasthan and other States. 
Retail prices of Rice, which were earlier showing steady trend around Rs. 15 per kg since the 
beginning of 2007, are now showing a firm trend since December 2007 and is now Rs. 18 per 
kg mainly owing to a hike in MSP and bonus declared by the Government. 
(b) Price rise in some food articles mainly rice, tur dal and edible oils is witnessed mainly 
due to inadequate suplies in relation to demand, diversion of foodgrains to bio-fuel and 
animal feed, production losses due to inclemen t weather conditions and food-inflation in 
international markets. The prices of essential commodiities from May 2004 to January 2008 
are given in the Annexure. 
[See Appendix 213 Annexure No. 3] 
(c) The Government has taken a number of steps to control the price rise and to soften the 
impact of price rise on consumers. The important steps taken are given below. 
(i) To augment availability of wheat Public Sector Agencies STC, MMTC, BEC are in 
the process of importing 23.0 lakh Mts) (+/-5%) during 2007-08. About 18.0 lakh 
tonnes of wheat have been contracted and almost the entire quantity has arrived 
in India as of 27.02.2008. Period of validity of import of wheat at zero duty was 
extended from 31.12.06 to 28.2.2007 and further to 31.12.07. It is now extended until 
further orders. 
(ii) Export of wheat has been banned w.e.f. 09.02.2007. The ban will remain inforce up 
to 31.12.2007. The ban is now extended until further orders. 
(iii) In order to maximize procurement of wheat and paddy, the Government has been 
increasing MSPs and announcing bonuses in the last 5 years. The Government 
has on 9.10.2007 made a decision to fix the MSP of wheat for crop year 2007-08 (to 
be marketed in RMS 2008-09) at Rs. 1000 per quintal. It also approved an incentive 
bonus of Rs. 100 per quintal during the Kharif Marketing Season 2007-08 for 
Paddy. Similarly, the export of non-basmati rice below Minimum Export Price of 
$5000 per MT has been banned by the Government. 
(iv) Government has protected vulnerable sections of society through Targeted Public 
Distribution System (TPDS) and Antodaya Anna Yojna (AAY). Under the TPDS, 
wheat, rice, sugar and kerosene oils ar e allocated to State Governments for 
distribution through the Fair Price Shops. The offtake of wheat and rice under

Questions of 7th March, 2008 
Targeted Public Distribution System (TPDS) and other welfare schemes (OWS) 
has, however, been going up. For TPDS, wheat and rice offtake have gone up from 
242 lakh tonnes in 2003-04 to 316 lakh tonnes in 2006-07. During the period April-
November 2007, 242.96 lakh tonnes wheat and rice has been allocated under 
TPDS. 
(v) The Central Issue Price for rice and wheat has not been revised since 1.7.2002. For 
wheat it remains at Rs. 4.15 per kg for BPL and Rs. 2per kg for AAY. For rice, it is 
Rs. 5.56 per kg for BPL and Rs. 3 per kg for AAY. 
(vi) Customs duty on import of pulses was reduced to zero on June 8, 2006 and the 
period of validity of import of pulses at zero duty has been extended from 31.3.07 
to 1.8.2007 and further to 31.3.09. 
(vii) A ban was imposed on export of pulses with effect from June, 22, 2006 (except 
export of kaubli chana w.e.f. 7.3.07). The period of validity of prohibition on 
exports of pulses, which was in itially upto 31.3.07 was further extended upto 
31.3.2008. 
(viii) As per initiative of Government, the State agencies (NAFED, PEC Ltd., MMTC 
and STC) are targeted to import 1.5 Million Metric Tonnes (MMT) of pulses. Out 
of the total contracts of 14.01 lakh tonnes made by these agencies, 10.75 lakh 
tonnes have arrived up to 12.02.2008. Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) had 
been asked to import edible oils and to augment edible oils availability in the 
domestic market, they have currently placed orders for import of 46,500 tons of 
palm oils and the entire quantity has arrived at Indian ports. 
(ix) W.e.f. 1.3.07, the import duty on crude sunflower oil was reduced from 65% to 50% 
and that of refined sunflower oil from 75% to 60%. Again, with effect from 23.7.07, 
the import duty on sunflower oil, both crude and refined, has been reduced and 
now stands at 40% and 50% respectively. 
(x) With effect from 13.4.07, the import duty on CPO was reduced from 60% to 50% 
and that on refined palm oil from 67.5% to 57.5 % w.e.f. 23.7.2007 the import duty 
on crude palm oil (CPO) has been further reduced to 45% and that on refined palm 
oil to 52.5%. The Government has also withdrawn the 4% additional countervailing 
duty on all edible oils. Prior to 24.1.07 the import duties were 70% and 80% 
respectively. 
(xi) With effect from 23.07.07, import duty on Soya oils has been reduced from 45% to 
40%. 
(xii) To increase the domestic availability of onion, NAFED increased the MEP from 
USD 250 PMT in March/April 2007 to US$ 495 PMT in October 2007. Since domestic 
prices of onion now show a declining trend. MEP has been successively reduced. 
Currently, MEP of onion is US$ 200 PMT. The export of onion was also put under 
license through designated canalizing agencies vide Notification No. 22 (RE-
2007)/2004-2009 dated 4th October 2007. This restriction has now been lifted 
w.e.f. 16.11.07 having regard to the increased availability of kharif onion.

Furthermore, Government, also organised sale of onion through mobile centres 
operated by Delhi Government, NAFED, Kendriya Bhandar as well as Mother

the outside price was Rs 22-24 per kg. 
(xiii) Steps were taken by Reserve Bank of India to reduce liquidity in the system by 
increasing the cash reserve ratio, first to 7% w.e.f. 6 August 2007 and then to 7.5% 
on 30 October, 2007. These steps have mopped up liquidity in the market of more 
than Rs. 30,000 crores. 
(xiv) As a measure of abundant precaution, Forward Markets Commission (FMC) has 
on 23.01.07, directed the three National Exchanges, namely (a) Multi Commodity 
Exchange of India Ltd., (b) National Commodity & Derivatives Exchange Ltd., 
(c) National Multi Commodity Exchange of India Ltd., to delist all contracts of tur 
and urad and to close out all outstanding positions in all Tur and Urad contracts 
at the closing price on 23.01.07. FMC has also stated that no further contract shall 
be launched without its prior approval and permission already granted to launch 
contracts in Urad and Tur stands withdrawn. 
(xv) Similarly, FMC has on, 27.2.2007, directed all the three National Exchanges that no 
new futures contracts in wheat and rice shall be launched. 
(xvi) To contain volatility in the futures prices of wheat, pulses, etc. Forward markets 
Commission (FMC) has taken required regulatory measures such as imposition of 
limits on open position, reduction in limits on daily price fluctuation and imposition 
of additional/special margins. 
(xvii) An Expert Committee has been set up under the Chairmanship of Shri Abhijt it Sen, 
Member, Planning Commission to study impact, if any, of the trading in forward 
markets on the prices of the commodities. 
(xviii) Keeping in view the prevailing price situation, the Central Government had issued 
a Central Order dated 29.8.2006 under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 to 
enable the State Governments to invoke Stock Limits in respect of wheat and 
pulses for a period of 6 months. By virtue of this Order, the State Governments/UT 
Administrations have been empowered to take effective action to bring out the 
hoarded stock of these items to ensure their availability to the common people at 
reasonable prices. Government has, on 1.9.2007, extended the validity of the Central 
Order by another six months. It has now been extended further by six months from 
1.3.08 till 31.8.2008.

840. SHRI M.V. MYSURAREDDY: Will the Minister of CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD 
AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there is any proposal to revamp and improve the Public Distribution System 
in the country particularly in the rural areas; 
(b) if so, the details of steps taken to improve the Public Distribution System in the 
country during the year 2007-08; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOODAND 
PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (DR. AKHILESH PRASAD SINGH): (a) to (c) Reforming of the 
Targeted Public Distribution System (TPDS) to improve its efficiency, accountability and 
effectiveness is an ongoing process. The Government has been taking up a series of measures 
to improve the TPDS in rural as well as urban areas. 
The TPDS is operated under joint responsibility of Central and State and UT Governments. 
The Central Government is responsible for procurement, storage and allocation of foodgrains 
upto the Principle Distribution Centres (PDC) in the States/UTs State and UT Governments 
are responsible for identification of BPL, families, issuance of ration cards to eligible families, 
lifting of foodgrains and distribution through the network of 4.94 lakh Fair Price Shops 
scattered all over the country.

Major steps taken by Government for improving the TPDS are these: 
(i) A 9-point action plan has been under implementation by State/UT Governments. 
This has resulted in improvemnt in its functioning in terms of detection and 
elimination of bogus/fake ration cards, involvement of Panchayati Raj Institutions 
(PRIs), setting up Vigilance Committee, door delivery of foodgrains, etc. 
(ii) Concurrent evaluation of TPDS has been taken up in 26 States and UTs through 
NCAER and IIPA, New Delhi. 
(iii) A revised Citizens' Charter has been issued in July, 2007 for adoption and 
implementation by State/UT Governments for facilitaing use by citizens of 
provisions of Right to Information Act, 2005 in relation to functioning of TPDS. 
(iv) To ensure that TPDS foodgrains reach the targeted families and to minimize scope 
for their diversion, APL allocations have been rationalized. 
(v) Training Programmes for TPDS functionaries and Awareness campaign for TPDS 
beneficiaries are being taken up. 
(vi) Computerization of TPDS has been initiated. 
(vii) Use of new technologies such as Global Positioning System is being piloted. 
(viii) Revised policy on distribution of wheat flour has been issued.

National rural health mission 
857. SHRIMATI MOHSINA KIDWAI: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government has evaluated the scheme and performance of the National Rural 
Health Mission; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the States which are lagging behind in the implementation of the Mission; 
(d) whether serious misappropriation of funds has been detected in some World Bank 
sponsored health programmes in the country; 

332    Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Starred and Unstarred 
Questions of 7th March, 2008 
(e) if so, which are those programmes and Government's reaction thereto; and 
(f) the parameters of evaluation/social audit etc. for the National Rural Health Mission 
and other health programmes in the country alongwith the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE 
(SHRIMATI PANAB AKALAKSHMI): (a) to (f) The National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) is 
an overarching umbrella initiative for esta blishing a functional, community owned, 
decentralized health delivery system with their sectoral convergence at all levels. 
The NRHM has in built protocols for financial and physical monitoring and evaluation. 
All constituents of NRHM have pooled their resources and an integrated MIS has been 
operationalised to facilitate the process. 
The parameters which are subject matter of evaluation/social audit include physical 
upgradation of facilities, improvements in availability of equipments, logistics and 
management, improved availability of human resources along with change in range and 
quality of service delivery at various levels. The progress on these parameters is benchmarked 
against baseline facility surveys. Community monitoring and concurrent external evaluations 
provide valuable inputs for triangulating the in house data and results of periodic thematic 
surveys. 
The Mission Steerting Group (MSG) of NRHM, comprises Union Ministers who are 
incharge of key determinants of health. Independent Public Health Experts of eminence are 
also members of this group. The sessions of MSG are forums for evaluation of progress of 
NRHM. Similar mechanism also exists at the state level. 
The Mentoring Group on ASH A and Advisory Group on Community Action (which have 
been constituted with leading NGOs as members) and the Regional Resource Centres are key 
institutions engaged in concurrent evaluation of NRHM. 
Many of the key strategies under NRHM like ASHA and JSY have also been evaluated 
with assistance of  external agencies. The fidelity of financial processes in some of the states 
have also been evaluated. 
A Common Review Mission (CRM) was also undertaken during November 2007 where 
independent teams went to 13 representative States, visited health facilities and interacted 
with community organizations. The reports of the CRM have been widely shared. 
All the States have established institu tional framework of NRHM and started 
operationalisation of various strategies. The capacities of all States for training and 
management are being augmented on priority and progress against key indicators is being 
monitored. 
The World Bank has undertaken a detailed implementation review of five health sector 
projects which were being implemented during periods varying from 1997 till 2006 end. Certain 
deficiencies have been highlighted in the report in rela tion to programmes including HIV/ 
AIDS, Revised National Tuberculosis Control Programme, Orissa Health System Project etc. 
To address the systemic deficiencies pointed out in the World Bank report relating to 
procurement, implementation and oversight a Joint Action Plan has been finalised after 
intensive discussions with the World Bank keeping in mind specific interventions and 
timelines.

NRHM has initiated the following architectural corrections in the public health delivery 
system: 
• NRHM has in-built institutional and financial monitoring mechanism, e.g., 
Programme Management Units (PMUs) at  State/District/Sub-district levels 
consisting of management, financial and IT experts.

and Sanitation Committees at the village level and Rogi Kalyan Samitis (Patients 
Welfare Societies) at sub-district and District Hospital levels consisting of 
representatives of Panchayati Raj Institutions, civil society and Government 
health functionaries.

buildings and purchase of equipments. 
• Capacity Building of States for decentralised procurement. 
• Electronic transfer of funds from Government of India to States and States to 
district and E-Banking for real time financial reporting and monitoring. 
In addition, in Centralized procurement, following corrective actions have been taken:

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE 
(SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) A st ate-wise list of number of cases of 
meningococcal meningitis as reported in the country during the year 2007 is placed at Statement-
I. (See below/ During 2008, from 1 st January 2008 to 29th February 2008, a total of 106 cases (88 
probable, 18 confirmed cases) and 12 deaths (3 probable and 9 confirmed) due tomeningococcal 
disease were reported. Out of these 42 (35 probable, 7 confirmed) cases and 7 deaths (6 probable 
1 confirmed) were reported from out of Delhi. From Delhi, there were 64 cases (53 probable, 11' 
confirmed) and 5 deaths (3 probable 2 confirmed) due to meningococcemia disease. 
(b) and (c) In the wake of reporting of meningococcal disease in Delhi and surrounding areas in 
National Capital Region (NCR), the Directorate General of Health Services, Ministry of Health and 
Family Welfare convened the meeting of an expert group of 13th February, 2008 to review the 
situation. The Expert group comprised of National Institute of Communicable Diseases (NICD), 
Indian Council for Medical Research (ICMR), Medical Superintendent of major hospitals of Delhi, 
MCD, NDMC and Delhi Government. It was observed that all the major hospitals are fully 
equipped to manage the cases of this illness, having sufficient stock of medicines and laboratory 
reagents. All the hospitals have been directed to ensure regular and timely reporting of cases to 
Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD), which has been identified as the nodal agency to 
coordinate all the activities. 
MCD has aleady initiated Information E ducation and Communication (IEC) measures. 
Chemoprophylaxis is being given to high-risk personnel such as health care/laboratory worker 
and close contacts of the cases. 
NICD is providing referral diagnostic services. NICD has tested 44 clinical samples received from 
different hospitals from 1 st January to 27th Feb., 2008. Out of 44,8 (18.2%) samples were found 
positive for serotype-A meningococos. 
To monitor the situation of the disease on day-to-day basis and to know the trend of the 
disease, the information on the meningococcal disease is being collected regularly from the 
control room, tablished at MCD office. Epidemiological analysis is being carried out by the 
NICD and the weekly report is being sent to MCD for taking further necessary action. 
NICD also provides technical guidelines to States neighbouring Delhi to prevent and 
control meningococcal diseases, including training and laboratory support to hospitals. NICD 
circulates CD Alert on the Meningococcal disease to all the affected States, which includes 
case definition, clinical profile management of cases, prevention and control measures for 
outbreaks. The CD alert has been sent to MHO (MCD) for ready reference and circulation to all 
the reporting units. 
Funds are released to states/UTs under Integrated Diease Surveillance Programme (IDSP), which 
is a decentralized state based surveillance project to detect outbreaks of epidemic prone diseases 
including meningococcal meningitis. A list of state-wise and year-wise release of funds to 
States/UTs is placed at Statement-II.

Pending cases of export permission 
869. DR. V. MAITREYAN: Will the Minister of  HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that many cases fo r registration/ NOC to manufacture/NOC to 
export and permission to manufacture new drugs are pending in the office of the Drug 
Controller General of India for more than two to three years; 
(b) if so, the reasons for such de lay to process the applications and the details of such 
pending cases under each category for the last three years, year-wise; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that only select ive cases are taken up for consideration and 
leaving a huge backlog for approvals in the department; 
(d) the steps being taken to clear the pendancy and when it is likely to be cleared; and 
(e) whether the Government proposes to introduce computerization of the licensing system 
in the commerce department to bring transparency and better efficiency in the functioning 
and if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE 
(SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (e) No, Sir, during last three years, the Office of 
the Drug Controller General of India received about 6000 applications for export, for which 
NOCs have already been issued. Besides expor t applications, about 5500 applications of 
various categories of new drugs which include investigational new drugs, new drug molecules, 
vaccines, biotech products, new fixed dose combinations, subsequent approvals, new dosage 
forms, new indications etc. were also received during the said period. Details of the drugs 
including fixed dose combinations, approved for the first time, during the last three years are 
available at website www.cdsco.nic.in . During the said period about 2000 subsequent 
approvals of new drugs, already approved in the country, have also been issued. Rest of the 
applications are under various stages of evaluation viz. clinical trial, bioequivalence study, 
laboratory testing, seeking further information from the applicants etc. 
The evaluation of new drug applications wh erein establishing safety and efficacy of 
the drug in humans is of paramount importance, is a complex process as per Schedule-Y 
under Drugs & Cosmetics Rules and varies acco rding to the nature of molecule/drug, 
published data and information furnished by the applicants. It involves examination of 
chemical & pharmaeceutical informations, anim al pharmacological & toxicoligical data, 
clinical data of safety & efficacy, laboratory testing etc. Depending upon the nature of the 
application, it may take on an average 3 to 5 years for an applicant to complete all phases 
of trials required for approval of investigational New Drug (i.e. a drug molecule not tested 
on human being anywhere in the world); about 1-3 years for the first time approval of the 
drug already approved elsewhere but requiring confirmatory clinical trial, and about 2-3 
months for subsequent applications for already approved drugs. This is however, subject 
to submission of all required data as per pr ovisions of Schedule-Y of Drugs & Cosmetics 
Rules. 
Government is planning to introduce computerization, to bring transparency and better 
efficiency in the functioning, when the proposed Central Drugs Authority (CD A) is in place. 
The Drugs and Cosmetics (Amendment)Bill, 2007 in this regard has already been introduced 
in the Parliament.

Statement 
Impact of Eradication Programmes and Remedial Action Taken from Time to Time 
1. Revised National TB Control Programme 
As per the available estimates, deaths due to TB have decreased from over 500,000 prior 
to year 2000 to fewer than 3 70,000 currently. As per latest estimates, about 1.8 million new TB 
cases occur every year. As per the available data deaths due to TB were 37639, 56587 and 
62539 during the years 2004-05,2005-06 & 2006-07 respectively. The increase is because of 
large number of patients put on treatment by the programme. The details of expenditure 
under the programme during 2004-05,2005-06 & 2006-07 are Rs. 133.63 crore, 187.70 crore& 
220.97 crore respectively. 
The programme is achieving the global target of cure rate of 85% amongst new sputum 
positive cases and case detection rate of 70% amongst such cases. Prevalence of tuberculosis 
(old and new cases) has declined from 570 cases per 100,000 population in 1990 to 299 cases 
per 100,000 population in 2005. The programme is well on its way to achieve MDGs (Millennium 
Development Goals) related to tuberculosis. 
2. National Cancer Control Programme 
An estimated 4.4 lakhs people die of cancer every year and about 7-9 lakh new cancer 
cases are detected every year. At any given point of time there are 2.5 million cancer patients 
in the country. The year-wise details of cancer patients/cancer deaths are not maintained 
centrally. 
The Year-wise expenditure under NCCP for 2004-05,2005-06 & 2006-07 are Rs. 59.00 crore, 
66.00 crore & 43.02 crore respectively. 
3. National Programme for Prevention and Control of Diabetes, Cardiovascular Diseases 
and Stroke 
The Pilot Phase of the National Programme for Prevention and Control of Diabetes, 
Cardiovascular Diseases and Stroke has been launched in 2008 only in 9 districts of 9 States 
and a sum of Rs. 49.16 lakh has already been released to each of the 6 States. As the pilot 
phase of the programme has been launched only in 2008, the question of assessment of the 
impact is premature. Diabetes is not a fatal disease and hence no figures of death due to that 
disease are centrally compiled. 
4. National AIDS Control Programme (NACP) 
It is estimated that there are 2 to 3.1 million HIV infected persons in the country. A total of 
5170 (1624 in 2005,1786 in 2006,1760 in 2007) deaths due to AIDS have been reported by the 
State AIDS Control Societies during the last 3 years. The total expenditure incurred under 
National AIDS Control Programme during the last 3 years is Rs. 422.25 crore, Rs. 532.70 crore, 
and Rs. 682.63 crore in 2004-05,2005-06 and 2006-07 respectively.

Closure of SSI Units 
885. PROF. P.J. KURIEN: Will the Minister of MICRO, SMALL AND MEDIUM 
ENTERPRISES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether number of SSI units have become sick and closed because of the competition 
from multinational and other major industries; 
(b) if so, the number of such units closed during the last three years; 
(c) whether Government has any action plan to strengthen the SSI sector; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF MICRO, SMALL AND MEDIUM ENTERPRISES (SHRI MAHAVIR 
PRASAD): (a) and (b) The Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) has 
no information on the number of micro and small enterprises (MSE) (erstwhile SSI units) 
which have became sick and closed because of competition from multinational and other 
major industries. However, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) compiles data on the sick MSEs 
who have availed loans from scheduled commercial banks. Accordingly to RBI, the number 
of sick MSEs during 2004-05,2005-06 and 2006-07 were 1,38,041, 1,26,824 and 1,14,132 
respectively. 
(c) and (d) Promotion and development of MSMEs is primarily the responsibility of State/ 
Union Territory (UT) Governments. To assist the States/UTs and supplement their efforts in 
this regard, the Central Government implements several schemes/programmes for promotion 
and development of MSEs. These, inter alia, include, (i) facilitating availability of credit 
mainly through public sector banks/institutions, (ii) assistance for (a) technology upgradation, 
(b) marketing, (c) integrated infrastructural  development, (d) comprehensive need-based 
development of clusters, and (iii) entrepreneurship development.  
Further, the Government has enacted the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises 
Development (MSMED) Act, 2006 to facilitate the promotion and development of micro, 
small and medium enterprises and enhancement of their competitiveness. The Act has come 
into effect from 2nd October, 2006. 
Revival of leaf-cup/plate industry 
886. SHRI B.J. P ANDA: 
MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR: 
Will the Minister of MICRO, SMALL AND MEDIUM ENTERPRISES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is proposed to revive the traditional leaf-cup/plate making as a self-
employment option in a big way to generate  additional employment opportunities in the 
country especially in the tribal dominated regions, to improve their economy; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) what is the action plan of the Centre to help the Orissa Government both physically 
and financially to develop this sector for the tribal community of this region? 
THE MINISTEROF MICRO, SMALL AND MEDIUM ENTERPRISES (SHRI MAHAVIR 
PRASAD): (a) and (b) The Government (in the Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium 
Enterprises) has been implementing inter alia the Rural Employment Generation Programme 

362    Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Starred and Unstarred 
Questions of 7th March, 2008 
(REGP) through the Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC) for assisting the 
entrepreneurs in establishing village industry (VI) units, including the traditional leaf-cup/ 
plate making units, in rural areas and small towns with population upto 20,000 inlcuding 
those in the tribal dominated regions of the country, by availing of margin money assistance 
from KVIC and loans from public sector scheduled commercial banks, selected regional rural 
banks, cooperative banks, etc., for projects with a maximum cost of Rs. 25 lakh. Leaf-cup/ 
platemaking units are promoted under the Forest based industry (FBI) Group' of the village

banks against the projects sanctioned in each State/Union Territory (UT). During 2007-08, it 
has been targeted to assist the setting up of 1849 VI units under the FBI Group wth a margin 
money assistance of Rs. 2113. 13 lakh throughout the country, including 54 projects in 
Orissa with a margin money assistance of Rs. 61.90 lakh. 29 projects are reported to have 
been established in Orissa during 2007-08 (upto February, 2008), by utilizing Rs. 21.32 lakh of 
margin money assistance.

Textile, is the leading organisation working for the development of Handicraft 
Sector including Bamboo and Cane Handicraft Products in the country from NER.

Statement 
Major achievements in R &D in steel sector during last three years 
A. Steel Authority of India Ltd. Technology Development 
• On-line Control of coking process in coke oven batteries resulting in reduction of 
energy consumption by 5% and improvement in coke strength by 0.5 points. 
• Curtain flame ignition system in sinter machines resulting in curtailment of specific 
gas consumption by 30%, increase in productivity by 10% and ensured 
consistency in sinter quality through uniform heating (+10°C) across the width of 
the sinter machine. 
• Automated secondary cooling system in continuous caster resulting in elimination 
of reheating crack in medium carbon, high carbon and SUP 11A grades of cast 
billet. 
• Development of round ingot technology for yield and quality improvement in 
wheels resulting reduction in the weight variation in blocks could be reduced from 
40 to 15 kg. increase in yield from 70 to 90% at ingot to block stage.

931. SHRI DHARAM PALSABHARWAL: Will the Minister of STEEL be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Indian Steel Alliance (ISA) has requested Government to 
ensure that steel producers get iron ore at competitive price to keep steel prices under check; 
(b) if so, the details of the suggestions of ISA and the action taken by Government on 
these suggestions; 
(c) whether predictions for long terms prices of iron ore is not very favourable; and 
(d) if so, steps being taken in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF STEEL (DR. AKHILESH DAS): 
..(a) and (b) The Indian Steel Alliance (ISA) has requested the Governmenf to initiate steps 
for conservation of iron ore in the country for the long term benefit of the domestic steel 
industry. The suggestions given by ISA inter-alia include imposition of ceiling and export 
cess on export of iron ore. The Government has already taken necessary steps in imposing 
export duty on iron ore at the rate of Rs. 300 per tonne on iron ore lumps and Rs. 300 per tonne 
on iron ore fines with more than 62% Fe content and Rs 50 per tonne on less than 62% Fe 
content. 
(c) and (d) The Growth in demand for steel has seen an up-trend in the spot prices of iron 
ore during the last one year and the trend is likely to continue, concurrent with the growth in 
demand for steel, Since the iron ore is a freely tradable commodity its prices are determined

imposed an export duty at the rate of Rs. 300 per tonne on export of all varieties iron ore 
lumps. Export duty has also been imposed at the rate of Rs. 300 per tonne on export of iron 
ore fines with more than 62% Fe content and at the rate Rs. 50 per tonne on export of iron ore 
fines with less than 62% Fe content.
